# Literature clarifies the sparse-history summary question

**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
**Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University  
**Scope:** Task2 literature preparation notes.

**Research question:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?

**The inspected evidence does not establish the answer to this exact question.** FAR-Trans supplies the financial dataset and purchase-ranking benchmark; FLARKO demonstrates LLM recommendation on that dataset; UPR and LangPTune supply language-profile methods. However, LangPTune's closest direct-history comparison favors **NoProfile-CL (NDCG@20 0.0543) over the 512-token profile (0.0494)** on Movie-TV. The financial-evaluation literature also shows why purchase prediction must be distinguished from profitability. Together, these results motivate a controlled, two-sided investigation rather than a claim that summaries already improve sparse-investor recommendations. All LangPTune experimental claims below refer to the **February 2025 arXiv v2 manuscript**, not an independently checked final CIKM text. ([LangPTune v2, §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FAR-Trans, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5); [Investors, §§7–8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

This synthesis uses all five evidence-note files in `research_notes/Sparse financial recommendation literature/` and the existing Task1 measurements. Source reading/access is inherited from those documented research records; this writing pass read the notes rather than reopening academic full texts. AI assistance: OpenCode, `openai/gpt-6-astra`. The user reports personally verifying **transaction7590224 and asset metadata**; personal paper verification remains pending. Detailed bibliographies, access boundaries and claim locators are in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md); the bounded gap and pending controls are in [research_gap.md](research_gap.md).

## Five studies cover the dataset, method and evaluation

The five core studies are selected for complementary relevance. **FAR-Trans** is the foundation; **LangPTune** is the nearest methodological prior work among those inspected; **FLARKO** is the nearest same-dataset LLM application; **UPR** establishes the review-to-profile and editability rationale; **Investors Are (Not) Always Right** provides directly relevant metric interpretation. **Conv-FinRe was also investigated**, but remains an optional contextual source because its ten-participant conversational simulation and utility-based relevance are less directly matched to this RQ. This is a relevance judgment within six inspected studies, not an exhaustive ranking of the literature.

### Professor-facing comparison table

| Study (authors, year, venue) | Problem/method | Data/evaluation | Limitation/link to RQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FAR-Trans: An Investment Dataset for Financial Asset Recommendation** — Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Nikolaos Droukas, Richard McCreadie (2024), IJCAI-24 **Fin-RecSys workshop** | Public financial recommendation dataset; 11 random, price, transaction and hybrid methods; binary acquisition history. | FAR-Trans; 61 temporal variants, six-month future novel acquisitions; nDCG@10 and monthly ROI@10. LightGCN **0.3404**, popularity **0.2710** nDCG@10. | Foundational dataset/protocol, not an LLM or sparse-cohort comparison. Reconstructed holdings complicate point-in-time interpretation; published aggregates are not class/sparse results. [§§3, 5; Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2) |
| **Aligning Language Models with Investor and Market Behavior for Financial Recommendations** — Fernando Spadea, Oshani Seneviratne (2025), **ICAIF '25**; FLARKO | Qwen3 receives personal/market KGs serialized as JSON-LD; KTO aligns recommendations with future purchases and positive returns; centralized/federated variants. | FAR-Trans; 180-day outcomes; Pref@3, Prof@3, Comb@3. Centralized best Comb@3 **0.3718 ± 0.0547**, 1.7B/**Nothing** context. | Same dataset and LLMs, but graph inputs are not generated narrative histories; no nDCG@10 or sparse-user result. Context removal changes information. Results read in arXiv v1; publication metadata separately verified. [§§3–7; Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2) |
| **Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles** — Jerome Ramos, Hossein A. Rahmani, Xi Wang, Xiao Fu, Aldo Lipani (2024), **ACL, Volume 1: Long Papers**; UPR | Generate first-person profiles from selected review features using Llama2/Mistral; GPT-2 predicts ratings from profile and item title; profile edits steer recommendations. | Amazon Movies and TV / TripAdvisor; ≥5 training reviews/user; RMSE, MAE, MAP and **condensed-list** nDCG@10. Best UPR nDCG **0.940 / 0.955**, MF **0.941 / 0.960**. | Feasible, editable profiles; no ranking superiority over MF here. Review-rich warm-start ratings differ from sparse financial purchase prediction; model and information differ across baselines. [§§3–5; Table 2, p.13977](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf) |
| **LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation** — Zhaolin Gao, Joyce Zhou, Yijia Dai, Thorsten Joachims (2025), **CIKM '25** | Jointly optimize LLM profile generator with RLSO and Mxbai embedding ranker with contrastive learning; compare direct-history NoProfile variants. | **Evidence: arXiv v2, differently titled** *End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles*. Amazon Movie-TV/Books; four history items → one future item; Recall/MRR/NDCG@20. Movie-TV NoProfile-CL **0.0543 > 0.0494** full 512-token profile. | Closest method/control evidence; compression can hurt. No FAR-Trans or pre-cutoff sparse cohort; review parity unresolved; separately trained rankers differ. Final CIKM tables not checked. [v2 §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4) |
| **Investors Are (Not) Always Right: A Comparison of Transaction-Based and Profitability-Based Metrics for Financial Asset Recommendations** — Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Richard McCreadie, Nikolaos Droukas, Craig Macdonald, Iadh Ounis (2026), **ACM TOIS 44(2), Article 51** | Formal metric analysis and 12-algorithm empirical comparison; tests whether purchase relevance substitutes for profitability. | FAR-Trans; 61 temporal variants, main six-month horizon; pooled nDCG@10/monthly ROI@10 correlation **−0.13**, approximately 1.5 million user × algorithm × date observations. | Supports purchase/return distinction, not summaries. No representation arm or sparse subgroup. Shared FAR-Trans baseline values are not an independent replication of summary gains. [§§6–8; Fig.4/Table 5](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7) |

## FAR-Trans anchors the task but leaves sparse-summary effects unmeasured

### Dataset construction matters to what a summary can truthfully say

Sanz-Cruzado, Droukas and McCreadie describe investment opportunities available to Greek investors through one large European financial institution, including stocks, bonds, mutual funds, asset prices, anonymized customers and buy/sell logs from January 2018 to November 2022. Table 1 reports **29,090 customers, 806 unique assets, 321 assets with investments, 703,303 price points, 388,049 transactions, 228,913 acquisitions and 159,136 sales**. The parenthetical “unique” transaction/acquisition counts in that table do not have a sufficiently explicit deduplication key to relabel them as distinct user–item pairs. Their qualified novelty claim concerns a public FAR dataset containing **both prices and investment transactions**, not the absence of all earlier public financial recommendation data. ([§§2.2–3/Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1))

The released events are **processed and partly reconstructed**, not all untouched observed purchases. The authors remove transactions lacking customer IDs, adjust shares for stock splits and insert cash-in-lieu sales for fractional shares after reverse splits. When end-2022 balances imply sales from pre-existing holdings, they recreate the missing buys at the earliest available price date, usually 2 January 2018. Transactions outside a price series are moved to its nearest covered date; remaining holdings can be closed when a price series ends; monetary values are estimated from adjusted shares and closing prices. Prices themselves are cleaned, euro-converted, split-adjusted and gap-filled. Customer risk/capacity can be estimated rather than questionnaire-observed. ([§3.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS1.SSS1); [§3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1); [§3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS4))

This creates a substantive representation issue: a fluent summary must not turn reconstructed holdings into certain dated purchase decisions or estimated profiles into confirmed preferences. Because some early-dated buys are reconstructed using end-of-release balances, a timestamp-before-cutoff filter alone does not prove contemporaneous observability. This is an **inferred point-in-time validity concern**, not a measured leakage effect. Equal treatment across representations is necessary for comparison, but does not by itself establish historical authenticity. ([Construction basis, §3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1))

### The published benchmark predicts new-to-user acquisitions

At recommendation time `t`, the formal target ranks assets from the available set excluding those the customer **bought before t**. Training uses past prices and transactions, with a binary acquisition matrix rather than graded spending/frequency ratings. The authors evaluate **61 time points**, beginning **1 August 2019**, described as “spaced two weeks apart”; they do not enumerate the complete schedule. Each point uses prior history and **six months of future acquisitions**. Assets purchased in both training and test contribute only to training. Customers must be active in both periods, and assets must have prices throughout the test period, aligning the population for purchase and profitability metrics. This is neither a random 80/20 protocol nor an unrestricted repeat-purchase task. ([§5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS1); [§5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1))

The stated candidate set is the available universe minus previously purchased assets, subject to test-pricing eligibility. The text does **not** establish a restriction to the 321 globally traded assets, a sampled-negative protocol, or exact per-window candidate counts. **nDCG@10** measures future-acquisition relevance. **ROI@10** is reported as the monthly average return of an equally weighted top-ten portfolio over the six-month horizon; **0.0259 means 2.59% monthly**, not a 2.59% six-month total. The original workshop text does not give the exact monthly conversion equation. Table 2 averages over evaluation time points; detailed within-window weights are unspecified. ([§§5.1–5.2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))

### Eleven methods provide substantial non-LLM benchmarks

The random baseline is accompanied by three price-based ROI regressors: **random forest, linear regression and LightGBM**, using indicators such as average price, past ROI, volatility, MACD, momentum, rate of change, RSI, detrended price oscillator, ROI/volatility and previous-period extrema. Transaction methods are **popularity**, **LightGCN**, **Apriori association-rule mining (ARM)**, **matrix factorization (MF)** and **user-based kNN**. Popularity is described as number of prior purchases; the paper does not fully reconcile event-count popularity with binary acquisition preprocessing. Two hybrids use recommender outputs as features: **LightGBM regression** for profitability and **LambdaMART/Hybrid-nDCG** for ranking. Neither hybrid uses generated text. All algorithms' hyperparameters are selected by **six-month ROI at 1 April 2019, 1 October 2019 and 31 January 2020**, including the model with an nDCG training objective. ([§5.2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS3))

The complete published Table 2 is reproduced below. ROI retains the paper's decimal monthly scale; market/customer rows are references, not additional algorithms. ([§5.3/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2))

| Family | Algorithm/reference | nDCG@10 | Monthly ROI@10 |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| None | Random | 0.0106 | 0.0071 |
| Prices | Random forest | 0.0237 | 0.0259 |
| Prices | Linear regression | 0.0215 | 0.0249 |
| Prices | LightGBM | 0.0221 | 0.0225 |
| Transactions | Popularity | 0.2710 | 0.0006 |
| Transactions | LightGCN | **0.3404** | 0.0004 |
| Transactions | ARM | 0.2556 | 0.0007 |
| Transactions | MF | 0.1780 | 0.0038 |
| Transactions | User-based kNN | 0.1599 | 0.0119 |
| Hybrid | Hybrid-nDCG | 0.2313 | 0.0063 |
| Hybrid | Hybrid-regression | 0.0261 | 0.0132 |
| Reference | Market average | — | 0.0079 |
| Reference | Customer average | — | 0.0018 |

**Only LightGCN exceeds popularity on nDCG in this comparison.** Its advantage is 0.0694 absolute, approximately 25.6% relative, calculated from the table, not an LLM effect or a significance claim. The best price model on ROI is poor at predicting purchases. The authors' conclusion explicitly separates profitable-asset discovery from predicting customer investments. Popularity therefore deserves serious attention in subsequent benchmark discussions, while the scores themselves are contextual published aggregates, not target scores for a sparse cohort. ([Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2); [§6](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S6))

### Sparsity motivation is stronger than sparse-user effect evidence

The paper states that **over 50% of users have three or fewer transactions over 2018–2022**. That is full-period total activity, not pre-cutoff Buy counts or distinct purchased assets. It reports no sparse-specific nDCG, summary arm, confidence intervals or significance tests for Table 2. Six-month windows at approximately fortnightly origins overlap, and the listed ROI-tuning dates are not all earlier than the first test origin. Exact date lists, seeds, per-window populations, tuning grids and nested chronological validation are not established in the inspected text. These are reproducibility/interpretation limits, not proof of a quantified implementation error. A single institution, concentrated asset popularity and one market period also bound transfer. ([§3.3.2/Fig.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS2); [§5.2–5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))

### Task1 supplies local context without defining the experimental cohort

The existing local inspection reports **388,048 transaction data rows**, **29,090 customers**, **320 traded ISINs**, **806 metadata ISINs**, and **807 price-series ISINs**. Table 1's transaction/traded-asset counts are **388,049 / 321**. The paper itself also mixes 806 in Table 1 and 807 in §3.2. One header makes the local CSV-record total 388,049, but that arithmetic does **not establish why the paper differs**. Local transaction dates extend to **30 November 2022**, whereas the institutional collection metadata ends **29 November**; prices locally end on 29 November. These distinctions remain unresolved rather than silently harmonized. ([Task1 inventory, “Customers, assets and transactions”](dataset_inventory.md#customers-assets-and-transactions); [Task1 date checks](data_quality_analysis.md#dates-and-numeric-checks); [paper Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1); [institutional dataset record](https://researchdata.gla.ac.uk/1658/))

Task1's full-release median is **three total events and two Buy events**; **21,237 customers (73.00%)** have 1–3 Buys, **23,663 (81.34%)** have 1–5, and **25,736 (88.47%)** have 1–10. These overlapping bands are descriptive only. Moreover, **360** customers in the 1–5 Buy band have more than ten total events, so purchase-sparse does not necessarily mean sparse buy/sell input. Task1's proposed 1–5 pre-cutoff Buy band remains provisional. It cannot be populated by reusing whole-release counts. ([Task1 sparse-user analysis](sparse_user_analysis.md))

Information equivalence must also account for measured metadata quality: among **836 asset metadata rows**, sector is blank in **388** and industry in **439**; **three ISIN/date keys** have conflicting records. Transaction IDs alone repeat, while `(customerID, transactionID)` is unique in the measured release. **12,501 customer-profile rows** have questionnaire dates later than their own snapshot timestamps. These are row/key-level observations, not counts of sparse users. They matter because summary generation can hide missingness, conflate records or add unsupported preference interpretations; the structured comparator should receive the same permitted, time-valid fields. ([Task1 data-quality analysis, missing values, key duplication and timing](data_quality_analysis.md))

## FLARKO supplies same-dataset LLM evidence, not a summary comparison

Spadea and Seneviratne's FLARKO constructs a **personal knowledge graph** with ISIN, buy/sell type, value and timestamp, and a **market knowledge graph** with price summaries and asset category/sector/industry. Both are triples serialized as **JSON-LD**, capped jointly at **5,000 triples**. Ten-week price summaries are numeric aggregations, not LLM-written transaction narratives. Events and completed price-summary periods precede the recommendation date. Qwen3 models receive these graphs and generate three ISINs for the next six months. **KTO** labels desirable recommendations using the intersection of an actual purchase within **180 days** and a positive asset return. The method therefore changes representation, ranking model and behavioral/profitability supervision together. ([arXiv v1, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S3))

The study uses FAR-Trans training data from **2 January 2018–30 November 2021**, with prompts every four weeks during **1 August 2019–1 June 2021**. Test data span **1 December 2021–29 November 2022**, with prompts every two weeks during **1 December 2021–2 June 2022** and 180-day outcome buffers. Qwen3 sizes are **0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and 8B**; centralized training uses three epochs, while simulated federated experiments use twenty clients and omit 8B for compute reasons. The **23,784 balanced labeled examples** are training examples, not a reported number of evaluated investors. The conventional baselines include random, price regressors and transaction-based popularity/CF/ARM methods. ([§6.1–6.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6))

Evaluation uses **Pref@3, Prof@3 and Comb@3**, described as Hits@3 against purchased, profitable and intersection sets. No nDCG@10 is reported. Table 2 gives **0.6B/PKG Pref@3 0.4439 ± 0.0355**, compared with **0.6B/Combined 0.0354 ± 0.0131**. The highest centralized preference score is **1.7B/MKG 0.5341 ± 0.0532**; highest profitability score is **4B/Combined 0.6400 ± 0.0554**; highest combined score is **1.7B/Nothing 0.3718 ± 0.0547**. These maxima belong to different configurations. The ± values are the caption's **standard errors of proportions**, not confidence intervals or across-seed standard deviations. ([§6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS3); [§7.1/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2))

The paper's broad conclusion that combining personal and market graphs yields the strongest results needs qualification: **Combined is below PKG on Pref@3 and Comb@3 for every centralized size**, and the best Comb@3 uses no explicit graph context. Section 7.1 acknowledges combined-context degradation. Section 7.3 compares selected best configurations with baselines and reports advantages on preference/joint hits, but exact graphical baseline differences were not digitized in the evidence notes. Nothing here shows that natural-language summaries outperform matched structured histories. ([§7.1–7.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7); [§8](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S8))

FLARKO is the **nearest application prior work**, but it has no pre-cutoff sparse-cohort analysis. PKG/MKG/Nothing ablations change information, and the text does not fully establish identical users/candidate lists across ablations, exact hit-rate denominators, repeat-purchase policy or invalid/duplicate-ISIN handling. These are verification gaps, not evidence that cohorts definitely changed. Its original v1 main text and local PDF were read during the evidence research; the ICAIF publication metadata is verified separately, while the final publisher text was blocked. ([§§6–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6); [ACM-deposited metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3768292.3770399))

## Language-profile studies expose benefits and information loss

### UPR supports editable review profiles, with competitive rather than superior ranking

Ramos, Rahmani, Wang, Fu and Lipani's **User Profile Recommendation (UPR)** extracts sentiment-bearing features from reviews, ranks them using rating-derived utility, coverage and significance, and prompts Llama2-7B or Mistral-7B to write a first-person profile. Defaults select **five features**, **five reviews per feature** and a **200-token** profile. A separately fine-tuned **GPT-2** predicts a rating from the profile and candidate item title. The generated profile is thus a compact, editable representation of explicit review sentiment, not a faithful serialization of transaction IDs, amounts and dates. ([ACL published PDF, §§3.2–3.4, 4.4; Appendix A](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

Amazon Movies and TV contains **4,811 users, 5,459 items and 288,693 records**; TripAdvisor contains **9,765 users, 6,280 items and 320,023 records**. The **8:1:1** split requires every user/item to appear in every split and at least **five training reviews per user**; no global chronological cutoff is established. RMSE/MAE evaluate ratings; MAP and nDCG@10 use **only explicitly rated test items in condensed lists**. Consequently, values near 0.94 cannot be compared with catalog-wide FAR-Trans purchase nDCG. ([§4.1/Table 1; §4.2, p.13975](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

Table 2 reports the following selected results. They are descriptive comparisons without a supplied equivalence test or uncertainty intervals for these pairs. ([Table 2, p.13977](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

| Model | Amazon RMSE | Amazon nDCG@10 | TripAdvisor RMSE | TripAdvisor nDCG@10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MF | 0.925 | **0.941** | 0.786 | **0.960** |
| UPR (Llama2) | 0.944 | 0.938 | 0.804 | 0.955 |
| UPR (Mistral) | 0.941 | 0.940 | 0.804 | 0.952 |

Profile quality was assessed by **five master's-student annotators**, fifty profiles per domain; relevance satisfaction was **90%/87%** for Amazon/TripAdvisor. An editing experiment with **200 users** and lists of **100 feature-matching plus 100 other items** found higher target-feature Coverage@10 after positive profile edits. This supports readability and steering, not future-purchase accuracy or financial utility. The authors also report hallucinated/inferred content, review dependence, loss of rare preferences and difficulties with negative preferences. ([§5.3/Table 3, §5.4; §§6–8; Appendix A.5–A.6](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

UPR belongs in the five-paper set because it concretely demonstrates the profile pipeline and its trade-offs. Its CF comparisons change architecture and available semantics, while the editing test intentionally adds preferences. Neither isolates the encoding of the same sparse history. Warm-start review selection and feature-count ablations are not pre-cutoff financial sparsity tests. ([§§3–5](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

### LangPTune is the nearest methodological precedent and a necessary counterexample

The verified CIKM publication is **LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation** by Gao, Zhou, Dai and Joachims. The experimental text read is the local **`2410.18870v2.pdf`**, titled **End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles**, dated **12 February 2025**. The initial preprint was submitted 24 October 2024; CIKM publication metadata dates to 10 November 2025. These are linked versions of the work, but final-table equivalence remains unchecked. ([Publication metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3746252.3761369); [official accepted papers](https://cikm2025.org/program/accepted-papers); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18870))

In v2, a **Gemma-2B-it or Llama-3-8B-Instruct** encoder generates a natural-language profile from historical item metadata and reviews. An **Mxbai embedding decoder** scores the profile against candidate metadata by inner product. **RLSO** optimizes the generator using downstream ranking rewards, while **contrastive learning (CL/InfoNCE)** trains the decoder; full LangPTune alternates both. This is task-optimized profile generation, not simply applying a fixed zero-shot summarizer. The variants freeze both components (-0), train only the decoder (-CL), or train only the generator (-RLSO). ([v2 §§3.1–3.2, 4.2–4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S3))

Amazon Movie-TV and Books examples contain **four distinct historical items and one distinct future item**, after filtering sessions/items with fewer than five interactions and overly long metadata/histories. Movie-TV has **14,698/1,392/1,392** train/validation/test sessions and **10,533 items**; Books has **4,404/361/361** sessions and **4,819 items**. Metrics are **Recall@20, MRR@20 and NDCG@20**. The short inputs are relevant to the RQ, but are not naturally sparse FAR-Trans cohorts selected before a shared calendar cutoff. Baseline access to validation/test history items, permitted by footnote 1, further differs from a simple globally chronological split; that is not by itself evidence of future-target leakage. ([v2 §4.1/Table 1; §4.2/footnote 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T1))

Joint training improves several language-profile baselines: Llama/Movie-TV NDCG@20 increases from **0.0231** (-0) to **0.0494** (full); Gemma/Books increases from **0.1743** to **0.2736**. The reported **113.9%** and **57.0%** relative gains compare optimized with zero-shot profile pipelines, **not summaries with structured histories**. Full LangPTune is not uniformly best against conventional models: Movie-TV **0.0494** is below LightGCN **0.0525** and MCL **0.0563**, whereas Books **0.2736** exceeds LightGCN **0.2586**. ([v2 Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T2))

The most relevant comparison bypasses profile generation: **NoProfile-0** directly embeds the historical item-metadata list with pretrained Mxbai; **NoProfile-CL** trains this direct-input decoder with InfoNCE. Table 4 gives the following **Movie-TV/Llama** results. ([v2 §4.5.1/Table 4, p.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4))

| Pipeline | Maximum profile tokens | Recall@20 | MRR@20 | NDCG@20 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| LangPTune | 64 | 0.0604 | 0.0201 | 0.0319 |
| LangPTune | 128 | 0.0901 | 0.0313 | 0.0444 |
| LangPTune | 256 | 0.0929 | 0.0352 | 0.0482 |
| LangPTune | 512 | 0.0970 | 0.0358 | 0.0494 |
| NoProfile-0 | — | 0.0760 | 0.0261 | 0.0372 |
| **NoProfile-CL** | — | **0.1012** | **0.0408** | **0.0543** |

**The best direct-history comparator exceeds the 512-token profile by 0.0049 NDCG@20.** Equivalently, the profile is approximately 9.0% below NoProfile-CL, arithmetic derived from the table; this pair has no reported significance marker. The authors explicitly discuss the language-profile information bottleneck. A limited fixed-decoder comparison also exists: **NoProfile-0 0.0372**, **LangPTune-0 0.0231**, and **LangPTune-RLSO 0.0377** use the pretrained decoder on Movie-TV. This is relevant partial control evidence and should not be dismissed, but reviews, formatting/truncation parity and significance of these exact contrasts remain unresolved. Full LangPTune versus NoProfile-CL instead uses separately trained decoder weights and different training settings. ([v2 Tables 2/4, §§4.2.1, 4.5.1; Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2))

Two other distinctions prevent overstatement. Reducing **global training-set size from 100% to 0.1%** is not a per-user sparsity experiment. The human interpretability test finds **58.89%** binary next-movie choice accuracy for trained profiles versus **57.11%** raw history and **54.67%** zero-shot profiles, with trained-versus-raw **p=0.624** and trained-versus-zero-shot **p=0.201**. Those nonsignificant comparisons and shorter reading times concern a readability/usefulness trade-off, not proof of superior ranking or faithful transaction summaries. ([v2 §4.5.2/Fig.4; §4.6/Tables 5–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.SS6))

## Financial evaluation bounds the meaning of an eventual result

### Investors Are (Not) Always Right separates predicting purchases from earning returns

Sanz-Cruzado, McCreadie, Droukas, Macdonald and Ounis compare transaction-based and customer-independent profitability metrics theoretically and empirically. Theorem 5.6 establishes **zero correlation over all possible valid user–ranking pairs at a fixed time/horizon**, under its assumptions. The authors use “independence,” but zero covariance alone is not general statistical independence; the safe substantive conclusion is **no guaranteed positive relationship**, not a universal law about actual investors. ([TOIS §5.3, Theorem 5.6](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-5-3))

The empirical study uses FAR-Trans and **twelve algorithms**, adding **customer profile similarity (CPS)** to the original eleven-method inventory. The main protocol has **61 temporal variants**, a six-month horizon, binary novel-acquisition relevance and test-activity/pricing filters. Hyperparameters are again selected for six-month ROI at the three dates described above. The article states origins from **1 August 2019 to end-November 2021**, spaced two weeks apart; those statements do not yield an unambiguous literal 61-origin schedule. A complete date list remains a reproduction question. CPS also uses demographic information that the article's Data Statement says could not be publicly shared. ([§6.1–6.3](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6); [Data Statement](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-13))

Unlike the workshop paper, this article supplies explicit metric equations: binary purchase gain with logarithmic rank discount, an equally weighted top-k portfolio, and monthly conversion **`(1 + ROI)^(30 / horizon_days) − 1`**. The reported pooled correlation between **nDCG@10 and monthly ROI@10 is −0.13**, over approximately **1.5 million user × algorithm × temporal-variant values**, with authors reporting **p < 0.05**. This is not a correlation over only twelve model means. Repeated users and overlapping horizons mean that the pooled count should not be treated automatically as independent observations; the literature notes did not recalculate the uncertainty. ([§6.2/Eqs.7–12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6-2); [§7/Fig.4, p.51:23](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

Table 5 repeats shared FAR-Trans baseline values, including **LightGCN 0.3404 nDCG / 0.0004 monthly ROI**, **popularity 0.2710 / 0.0006**, and **random forest 0.0237 / 0.0259**. CPS gives **0.2722 / 0.0026**. These are useful metric contrasts, not a second independent demonstration of representation gains. The article's synthetic effective-investor experiment changes the pooled correlation to **+0.13**; date-specific correlations vary approximately **−0.65 to +0.4**. Thus a universally negative empirical relation is also unsupported. ([§8.1/Table 5](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#tab5); [§9.2/Fig.7](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-9-2); [§10/Fig.8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-10))

Limitations include one institution, partial portfolios, omitted dividend/coupon income, equal-allocation/customer-independent profitability and simplified common investment horizons. The authors explicitly say abandoning transaction-based evaluation is premature. For this RQ, improved nDCG@10 would mean **better ranking of future observed purchases**, not necessarily higher profits, suitability, risk reduction or welfare. The article contains no LLM-summary experiment or sparse-specific representation result. ([§12 and limitations](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-12))

### Conv-FinRe is an investigated alternative with a different target

**Conv-FinRe: A Conversational and Longitudinal Benchmark for Utility-Grounded Financial Recommendation** is verified as a **SIGIR 2026** publication. Experimental claims here use **arXiv v2**, a pre-camera-ready version. The publisher-deposited record has **thirteen authors**, while the arXiv version has **fourteen**, including **Rosie Guo** rather than the publication's **Yuqing Guo**, and **Xue Liu**, absent from the publication metadata. Their identities/reasons for the differences are not inferred; both full lists appear in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md#6-conv-finre--investigated-alternative). ([Publisher-deposited record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3805712.3808658); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16990))

This benchmark combines real market prices with **ten human participants' simulator decisions**, not FAR-Trans brokerage purchases. Ten stocks and **23 steps per user** yield **230 prefix-conditioned instances**, **270 unique turns** and **3,450 prefix-expanded turns**. Onboarding and later dialogues are generated from profiles and decision trajectories, rather than collected natural human-advisor conversations. Models rerank the fixed stock set using profile/history, market and advisor information. Utility combines standardized seven-day return with individual volatility/drawdown penalties, whose parameters are fitted over each participant's **full longitudinal trajectory**. ([v2 §§3.1–3.3/Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3))

Metrics include **utility-gain uNDCG over the full candidate set**, choice MRR/HR@1/HR@3 and Kendall τ against advisor rankings. Table 4 reports **Llama-3.3-70B uNDCG 0.97 ± 0.00**, while the finance-specific **XuanYuan3** has **MRR 0.65 ± 0.03** and **HR@1 0.54 ± 0.03**. The inspected caption/text does not clearly identify the ± estimator, so these are retained as reported uncertainty, not relabeled standard errors. History/no-history results are model-dependent: some improve, some barely change, and some lose utility alignment. Removing history changes information; it is not a summary-versus-structured contrast. ([v2 §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS4); [Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.T4); [§4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.SS3))

The small repeated-prefix sample, generated dialogue and retrospective utility calibration limit transfer. Full-trajectory fitting raises a point-in-time question if adapted to prospective prediction, without establishing a measured leakage effect in this diagnostic benchmark. The signed-utility equations do not document a nonnegative gain transformation, so conventional binary-nDCG bounds cannot be assumed; **0.97 is not comparable with FAR-Trans's 0.3404**. This paper is retained as adjacent evaluation context and excluded from the core five because Investors supplies more direct FAR-Trans metric evidence, while LangPTune better addresses the representation question. ([v2 §§3.2–3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS2); [§5](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S5))

## The preparation supports a bounded, two-sided research gap

**Among the studies inspected, we did not find a same-information comparison of LLM-generated transaction-history summaries versus structured-history features for a pre-cutoff sparse FAR-Trans cohort, evaluated on future-purchase nDCG@10 under matched users, candidates and downstream ranking conditions.** LangPTune is the closest methodological precedent because it tests bypassing the profile generator, including frozen-decoder variants; FLARKO is closest in dataset/application. Neither establishes the requested financial effect. UPR's lower nDCG than MF, LangPTune's direct-history advantage and FLARKO's mixed context results make a negative or null outcome scientifically informative. No expected effect size can be transferred across their different relevance definitions, cutoffs and candidate sets. ([LangPTune v2 Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FLARKO Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2); [UPR Table 2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

The remaining preparation task is to clarify the permitted comparison once the class protocol is available: historical information, sparse counting unit, new versus repeat purchases, candidate availability and what “fixed ranker” means. [research_gap.md](research_gap.md) records these as **pending controls**, not an approved experiment or an invented official split.

66:

68: 
69: The class cutoff/split, horizon, sparse threshold, candidate policy, repeat-purchase rule and allowed feature sources remain pending. FAR-Trans's **61 temporal variants from 1 August 2019** and FLARKO's **December 2021–2022 test interval** are each source-specific protocols. 70: 
71: The RQ remains about **purchase prediction, not profit**. A positive result would still require the control checks above before attributing it to representation. 74: 
75: **Provenance:** AI-assisted synthesis by OpenCode (`openai/gpt-6-astra`) from the existing evidence notes and Task1 outputs. The user personally verified transaction7590224 and asset metadata; personal paper verification is pending. No numerical effect for the proposed FAR-Trans comparison has been measured in this preparation.

- [ ] **Fixed item information:** provide the same permitted asset attributes and time-valid snapshots to both representations and candidate encoders. Record missing/conflicting fields identically; do not grant only the summary access to external asset descriptions, future prices or complete-release metadata.
- [ ] **Fixed train/history window:** use identical pre-cutoff events and history duration, with the same timestamp boundary, event types and treatment of repetitions. Separate training, validation and future outcomes chronologically according to the forthcoming class protocol. Filter before fitting preprocessing, computing popularity or generating summaries.
- [ ] **Baseline information equivalence:** the structured comparator must be allowed the **same underlying event fields and metadata**, including amounts, units, timing and buy/sell status if the summary sees them. A summary using extra risk profiles, market context or external knowledge tests augmentation as well as representation. Conversely, compare against meaningful structured history rather than an artificially information-poor baseline. Compression losses are part of the treatment; unequal source access is a confound.
- [ ] **Fixed downstream ranker:** explicitly distinguish **identical frozen fitted weights** from **the same scoring architecture/objective with separate fitting**. Both can be informative, but make different claims. Declare representation-specific adapters and their capacity; hold candidate representations, tuning budget and fitting conditions comparable. Sharing the Mxbai name alone is not fixed-weight control.
- [ ] **Fixed purchase target:** clarify novel assets only versus repeat purchases, future horizon, Buy relevance, aggregation and zero-relevant-user treatment. Both arms use identical labels and **nDCG@10**. FAR-Trans's published new-to-user six-month task is not automatically the class task.
- [ ] **Pre-cutoff sparse counting unit:** declare all transaction events, Buy events or distinct bought assets, and whether a finite history window applies. If both buys and sells enter summaries, report total historical events as well as Buy counts. Recompute after the official cutoff/item scope is known; do not select on full-release activity.
- [ ] **Matched historical provenance:** treat reconstructed/adjusted events and estimated fields consistently in both arms. Separate an event's assigned date from evidence it was actually known then. Avoid verbalizing inferred holdings or risk traits as directly observed facts.
- [ ] **Controlled summary generation:** record model/version, prompt, decoding and length limits; ground summaries in permitted records and assess unsupported additions/omissions. Check external/pretraining knowledge asymmetry. Fluency or shorter reading time alone is not faithfulness or predictive accuracy.
- [ ] **Paired and temporally aware assessment:** compare nDCG differences on matched instances; account for recurrent users and overlapping windows when later estimating uncertainty. Clarify model/tuning randomness. No independent-replicate count or significance test is chosen from the paper's overlapping 61 windows by assumption.
- [ ] **Contextual baselines and interpretation:** retain popularity as a serious benchmark consideration given the published 0.2710 aggregate nDCG@10, while distinguishing such external baselines from the primary same-information representation contrast. State negative, null and positive results with their uncertainty and cohort scope.

These controls are **inferences for later preparation**, not procedures already validated for the exact RQ. LangPTune supplies partial frozen-decoder evidence but does not certify input parity; FLARKO changes context/supervision; FAR-Trans and Investors compare different model/data families. ([LangPTune v2 §§4.2, 4.5/Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2); [FLARKO §§3–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1); [FAR-Trans §5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2); [Investors §6](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6))

## No official split or expected improvement is inferred

The class cutoff/split, horizon, sparse threshold, candidate policy, repeat-purchase rule and allowed feature sources remain pending. FAR-Trans's **61 temporal variants from 1 August 2019** and FLARKO's **December 2021–2022 test interval** are each source-specific protocols. Investors' additional last-origin statement does not resolve the exact date-list inconsistency. None is promoted to an official class split. Published aggregate LightGCN **0.3404** is not an expected sparse-cohort replication score. ([FAR-Trans §5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1); [FLARKO §6.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS1); [Investors §6.1](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6-1); [Task1 protocol status](dataset_inventory.md#sources-read-and-scope))

The RQ remains about **purchase prediction, not profit**. A positive nDCG@10 difference would support better ranking of subsequently bought assets under the declared protocol; it would not establish better investment returns, risk suitability, causal adoption, interpretability or welfare. Investors reports pooled nDCG/monthly-ROI correlation **−0.13** and cautions against treating one metric family as a proxy for the other, while explicitly retaining transaction evaluation as useful. ([Investors §§7, 12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

**Negative and null outcomes would be informative.** A negative result under matched conditions would show that the chosen summary pipeline loses or distorts useful predictive information in that cohort; it would not refute every possible language representation. A null estimate with wide uncertainty would be inconclusive, whereas a sufficiently precise near-zero estimate would constrain plausible benefit for the tested setting. A positive result would still require the control checks above before attributing it to representation. LangPTune's compression result makes this a substantive empirical question, not an exercise with a predetermined favorable answer. ([v2 §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4))

**Provenance:** AI-assisted synthesis by OpenCode (`openai/gpt-6-astra`) from the existing evidence notes and Task1 outputs. The user personally verified transaction7590224 and asset metadata; personal paper verification is pending. No numerical effect for the proposed FAR-Trans comparison has been measured in this preparation.

The PDFs are accessible in the **Session 1 directory**; `Papers/` itself is empty. I used the supplied copies to continue and **complete Task 2**.

## Generated files

- [results/literature_review.md](results/literature_review.md) — professor’s five-study comparison table, paper-by-paper findings, FAR-Trans algorithms and evaluation results, and assessment of Conv-FinRe.
- [results/reference_verification.md](results/reference_verification.md) — complete bibliographies, verified DOIs, source URLs, supporting sections/tables, PDF versions and access limitations.
- [results/research_gap.md](results/research_gap.md) — nearest prior work, bounded research gap and requirements for a controlled comparison.

## Selected studies

| Study | Verified venue/year | DOI |
|---|---|---|
| **FAR-Trans** | Fin-RecSys workshop at IJCAI, 2024 | [10.48550/arXiv.2407.08692](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2407.08692) — arXiv DOI; separate proceedings DOI not verified |
| **FLARKO** | ICAIF, 2025 | [10.1145/3768292.3770399](https://doi.org/10.1145/3768292.3770399) |
| **Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles** | ACL, 2024 | [10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.753](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.753) |
| **LangPTune** | CIKM, 2025 | [10.1145/3746252.3761369](https://doi.org/10.1145/3746252.3761369) |
| **Investors Are (Not) Always Right** | ACM TOIS, 2026 | [10.1145/3780097](https://doi.org/10.1145/3780097) |

**Conv-FinRe** was also investigated. It is less directly matched to your RQ because it uses a conversational simulator benchmark and utility-based evaluation rather than FAR-Trans future purchases.

## Main findings for your RQ

- **FAR-Trans establishes the dataset and non-LLM benchmark.** Its published aggregate nDCG@10 is **0.3404 for LightGCN** and **0.2710 for popularity**. These are not sparse-user results or expected scores under the pending class protocol.
- **LangPTune is the nearest methodological prior work.** Importantly, its accessible v2 manuscript reports **NoProfile-CL NDCG@20 = 0.0543**, versus **0.0494** for its 512-token profile pipeline on Movie-TV. This is evidence that summarization can lose useful information—not a direct result about structured financial features.
- **FLARKO is the nearest same-dataset LLM study.** It uses JSON-LD knowledge graphs and alignment training, evaluated with purchase/profitability Hits@3 variants. It does not establish your summary-versus-structured nDCG@10 comparison.
- **Predicting purchases is distinct from predicting profitability.** The financial-evaluation paper supports keeping those claims separate.

### Supported gap

> Among the studies inspected, we did not find an information-matched comparison establishing whether LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve future-purchase nDCG@10 over structured-history features for FAR-Trans users defined as sparse using pre-cutoff history.

This is a bounded finding, **not a first-ever novelty claim**.

### Version and verification qualifications

`2410.18870v2.pdf` is the earlier-title LangPTune manuscript, *End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles*. Its experimental findings are labelled **v2 results**, while the final CIKM publication metadata and DOI are verified separately. Final publisher-text equivalence remains unchecked for LangPTune, FLARKO and Conv-FinRe.

Your personal transaction and asset-metadata verification is acknowledged. **Personal paper verification remains pending.** No final homework report has been written.

**Stopping here for your review.**

# LLM4Rec Homework 1 — Session 1## Task 3: Research Importance, Business Value and Minimal Study Design


**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
**Dataset:** FAR-Trans  
**Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University


### Primary Research Question (RQ1)


Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?


## Background


Tasks 1 and 2 have been completed using OpenCode.


Task 1:
- Inspected the original FAR-Trans dataset.
- Calculated transaction statistics and sparse-user distributions.
- Identified temporal leakage and data-quality risks.
- Verified transaction ID 7590224 and its associated asset metadata.
- The student independently confirmed this transaction and asset metadata using Linux terminal commands.


Task 2:
- Investigated five academic research papers.
- Created a literature comparison.
- Checked publication details and relevant findings.
- Identified a provisional research gap.
- Conducted AI-assisted verification against the original PDFs.


The student's personal verification of all five papers has not yet been confirmed. Do not claim otherwise.


## Required Sources


Read the existing project files and results:


1. `session1_research_question_instructions (2).md`
2. `results/dataset_inventory.md`
3. `results/verified_transaction.md`
4. `results/sparse_user_analysis.md`
5. `results/data_quality_analysis.md`
6. `results/literature_review.md`
7. `results/reference_verification.md`
8. `results/research_gap.md`


Use the five research papers already investigated:


1. Sanz-Cruzado et al. (2024), FAR-Trans.
   https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08692


2. Fernando Spadea and Oshani Seneviratne (2025), FLARKO.
   https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15993


3. Jerome Ramos et al. (2024), Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles.
   https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753/


4. Gao et al. (2025), LangPTune.
   https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18870


5. Sanz-Cruzado et al. (2026), Investors Are (Not) Always Right.
   https://doi.org/10.1145/3780097


Verify every claim against the available primary sources.


Do not invent citations, findings, numerical results, or experimental evidence.


---


# PART A — Research Importance versus Business Value


Follow Section 7 of the professor's official instructions.


Develop TWO separate, academically grounded arguments.


## A1. Research Importance


Explain:


1. Why sparse-history financial asset recommendation is a meaningful research problem.
2. What existing research has established.
3. What remains unanswered by the five reviewed studies.
4. Why comparing structured histories with LLM-generated summaries is scientifically meaningful.
5. What a positive experimental result would establish.
6. What a negative or null result would establish.
7. How the proposed experiment contributes knowledge to LLM-based recommendation research.


Connect the arguments to FAR-Trans, FLARKO, the natural-language user-profile studies and the documented research gap.


Avoid exaggerated novelty claims.


## A2. Business Value


Identify a specific stakeholder, such as a financial recommendation product owner or an investment advisory team.


Explain:


1. What practical decision the stakeholder faces.
2. Why sparse transaction histories can affect personalization.
3. How LLM-generated summaries might help.
4. What additional computational costs, latency and operational risks they introduce.
5. What decision a positive result would support.
6. What decision a negative or null result would support.


Important:


- Future purchases are behavioral labels.
- nDCG@10 does not measure investment profitability.
- Do not claim improved financial returns, revenue or causal business outcomes.
- Do not present the system as personal financial advice.
- Support the argument with appropriate academic references.


Prepare concise, separate paragraphs suitable for Section 1 of a maximum-five-body-page academic report.


Also prepare brief discussion implications for Section 5.


---


# PART B — Complete the 12-Field Minimal Study Design


Follow Section 8 of the professor's official instructions.


Create a professional Markdown table with exactly these 12 required fields:


1. RQ and scope
2. Evaluated users and subgroups
3. Data fields used
4. Baseline(s)
5. Proposed method
6. Ablations and controls
7. Primary metric
8. Secondary metrics
9. Seeds, repeats and cost
10. Feasibility in four sessions
11. Ethical and leakage risks
12. Current state


Complete every field with a concrete, defensible proposal.


Do not leave any field blank.


Do not use unexplained TBD values.


## Experimental Comparison


**Arm A — Baseline**


Represent the user's historical financial transactions using structured features.


Possible features include:


- Historical Buy frequency
- Asset-category distribution
- Transaction recency
- Historical transaction value
- Historical asset preferences


Use only information available before the prediction cutoff.


**Arm C — Proposed Method**


Generate a concise natural-language summary of the same historical transactions using an LLM.


Use that summary as a user representation for the recommendation pipeline.


The comparison must isolate the effect of historical user representation as closely as possible.


Both methods must use:


- Identical eligible users
- Equivalent historical information
- Identical candidate asset sets
- Identical available item metadata
- The same downstream scoring architecture, with representation-specific input encoders documented
- Identical evaluation windows
- The same primary metric


Where feasible, include:


**Arm B — Additional Control**


A deterministic textual representation of the same historical transactions without LLM summarization.


Explain how this ablation distinguishes benefits from language formatting versus benefits from LLM-generated abstraction.


Maintain exactly one primary research question.


## Sparse-History Definition


Use actual FAR-Trans dataset statistics.


Provisionally define sparse users using 1–5 historical Buy transactions before each prediction cutoff.


Explain why this threshold is provisional.


Consider separate cold-start, light-activity and heavy-activity subgroups where evaluation eligibility permits.


Do not calculate sparse-user eligibility using transactions from the future evaluation period.


## Data Fields and Genuine Record


Use the personally verified transaction:


`transactionID = 7590224`


Source:


`FAR-Trans/transactions.csv`


Preserve the exact original fields and values.


Matching asset:

`industry = Utilities - Renewable`

Distinguish observed, predicted and missing information.


Do not invent the official training/test split.


## Evaluation


The shared deliverable is a Top-10 ranked list of financial assets per evaluated user.


The primary metric is:


**nDCG@10 against future asset purchases.**


Specify:


- How historical transactions are separated from future outcomes.
- How candidate assets are selected.
- How both experimental arms are evaluated fairly.
- How sparse-history subgroups are compared.
- How results will be aggregated.
- How uncertainty and repeated runs will be reported.


The instructor's official evaluation split, candidate universe and eligibility protocol are pending.


State provisional assumptions explicitly.


Do not invent official benchmark rules.


## Seeds, Repeats and Costs


Propose a realistic experimental plan.


Include:


- Three reproducible random seeds.
- Repeated experiments where randomness affects outcomes.
- LLM model and version documentation.
- Fixed prompts and generation parameters.
- An initial small-scale pilot.
- Estimated computational runtime.
- An explicit provisional budget ceiling.

Clearly distinguish proposed costs from measured costs.


Do not invent results.


## Four-Session Feasibility

Dataset exploration, literature review, research question and experimental design.


Session 2:
Structured-history baseline and evaluation pipeline.


Session 3:
LLM-generated summaries, controlled comparison and ablation studies.


Session 4:
Repeated experiments, statistical analysis, reproducibility and final reporting.


Keep the proposed study realistic within four sessions.


## Ethical and Leakage Risks


Explicitly address:


- Financial data privacy
- Re-identification risks
- Hallucinated investor preferences
- LLM pretraining-data contamination
- Future transaction leakage
- Reconstructed historical purchases
- Future asset-price leakage
- Predicted customer risk profiles
- Stale customer information
- Missing values
- Duplicate transaction identifiers
- Market regime changes


Specify practical safeguards rather than merely listing risks.


---


# PART C — Current Research State


Accurately describe what has been completed.


Completed:
- Dataset inspection
- Data-quality analysis
- Genuine transaction verification
- AI-assisted literature review
- Preliminary research-gap identification


Not completed:

- Quantitative A-versus-C comparison


Do not claim that recommendation models have already been trained.


Do not invent experimental findings.


Identify the next concrete implementation task.


---


# PART D — Required Output Files

**3. `results/evaluation_plan.md`**

Ensure the documents are consistent with one another and with the official homework requirements.


---


# PART E — Research Integrity and Final Validation


Before completing Task 3:


1. Check all 12 design fields against the official instructions.
2. Check that research importance and business value are separate.
3. Verify that every citation corresponds to an actual paper.
4. Check that the official FAR-Trans paper is included.

**Do not write the final PDF report yet.**

- The project must fit **four sessions**; if it does not fit, cut the question, not the evaluation.

- **LLM knowledge contamination** is a real risk: state the model, version, knowledge cutoff, and how you control for content the model may have seen during pretraining.
- Secondary data and historical confounds — market regime, survivorship, stale profiles — must be named in the report, not discovered in the results.

| Time-dependent asset metadata | Asset timestamps span 2018-01-01 to 2022-10-31; repeated ISINs and composite-key checks are above. | As-of join only metadata known by prediction time; do not backfill later versions. Resolve same-date conflicts and leave unavailable attributes missing. Last-update stamps alone do not prove archival availability. |
| Risk profiles and investment capacity | Customer snapshots repeat; riskLevel and investmentCapacity contain explicitly Predicted_ values and missing markers. | Prefer history-only inputs for the first comparison unless provenance is established. If included, use time-valid snapshots identically in both arms, retain observed/predicted/missing distinctions, and do not infer actual wealth or risk tolerance. |
| Predicted values | The README says Predicted_ risk/capacity values are algorithmic; their training data and fit dates are not supplied. | An apparently old row may still contain estimates based on later information. Exclude unverified estimates from the main historical comparison or justify provenance and test a declared ablation. |
| Questionnaire dates | 12,501 profile rows have lastQuestionnaireDate > timestamp; 7,275 use 2000-01-01. questionnaires.csv contains no user answers. | A timestamp-only join is insufficient. Require known questionnaire availability as well as snapshot availability; quarantine inconsistent/unknown cases pending clarification. Merely setting effective time to the later date is conservative but not proof of historical availability. |
| Future prices and full-period returns | Close prices extend to 2022-11-29. limit_prices contains maxDate, priceMaxDate and full-series profitability. | Omit full-series price summaries from history features. | LLM contamination and information asymmetry | The homework names these risks; no LLM summaries or recommendations have been generated in this inspection. | Later record model/version/knowledge cutoff, ground summaries in permitted inputs, avoid external future facts, and give the structured baseline the identical underlying information. |

No cleaning is applied. These checks are screening diagnostics, not a certification of correctness or profitability. No recommendation model is trained and no split is invented.

1: # Literature clarifies the sparse-history summary question
2: 
3: **Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
4: **Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University  
5: **Scope:** Task2 literature preparation notes.
6: 
7: **Research question:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?
8: 
9: **The inspected evidence does not establish the answer to this exact question.** FAR-Trans supplies the financial dataset and purchase-ranking benchmark; FLARKO demonstrates LLM recommendation on that dataset; UPR and LangPTune supply language-profile methods. However, LangPTune's closest direct-history comparison favors **NoProfile-CL (NDCG@20 0.0543) over the 512-token profile (0.0494)** on Movie-TV. The financial-evaluation literature also shows why purchase prediction must be distinguished from profitability. Together, these results motivate a controlled, two-sided investigation rather than a claim that summaries already improve sparse-investor recommendations. All LangPTune experimental claims below refer to the **February 2025 arXiv v2 manuscript**, not an independently checked final CIKM text. ([LangPTune v2, §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FAR-Trans, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5); [Investors, §§7–8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

11: This synthesis uses all five evidence-note files in `research_notes/Sparse financial recommendation literature/` and the existing Task1 measurements. Source reading/access is inherited from those documented research records; this writing pass read the notes rather than reopening academic full texts. AI assistance: OpenCode, `openai/gpt-6-astra`. The user reports personally verifying **transaction7590224 and asset metadata**; personal paper verification remains pending. Detailed bibliographies, access boundaries and claim locators are in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md); the bounded gap and pending controls are in [research_gap.md](research_gap.md).

13: ## Five studies cover the dataset, method and evaluation
14: 
15: The five core studies are selected for complementary relevance. **FAR-Trans** is the foundation; **LangPTune** is the nearest methodological prior work among those inspected; **FLARKO** is the nearest same-dataset LLM application; **UPR** establishes the review-to-profile and editability rationale; **Investors Are (Not) Always Right** provides directly relevant metric interpretation. **Conv-FinRe was also investigated**, but remains an optional contextual source because its ten-participant conversational simulation and utility-based relevance are less directly matched to this RQ. This is a relevance judgment within six inspected studies, not an exhaustive ranking of the literature.
