26: 
27: ## FAR-Trans anchors the task but leaves sparse-summary effects unmeasured
28: 
29: ### Dataset construction matters to what a summary can truthfully say
30: 
31: Sanz-Cruzado, Droukas and McCreadie describe investment opportunities available to Greek investors through one large European financial institution, including stocks, bonds, mutual funds, asset prices, anonymized customers and buy/sell logs from January 2018 to November 2022. Table 1 reports **29,090 customers, 806 unique assets, 321 assets with investments, 703,303 price points, 388,049 transactions, 228,913 acquisitions and 159,136 sales**. The parenthetical “unique” transaction/acquisition counts in that table do not have a sufficiently explicit deduplication key to relabel them as distinct user–item pairs. Their qualified novelty claim concerns a public FAR dataset containing **both prices and investment transactions**, not the absence of all earlier public financial recommendation data. ([§§2.2–3/Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1))
32: 
33: The released events are **processed and partly reconstructed**, not all untouched observed purchases. The authors remove transactions lacking customer IDs, adjust shares for stock splits and insert cash-in-lieu sales for fractional shares after reverse splits. When end-2022 balances imply sales from pre-existing holdings, they recreate the missing buys at the earliest available price date, usually 2 January 2018. Transactions outside a price series are moved to its nearest covered date; remaining holdings can be closed when a price series ends; monetary values are estimated from adjusted shares and closing prices. Prices themselves are cleaned, euro-converted, split-adjusted and gap-filled. Customer risk/capacity can be estimated rather than questionnaire-observed. ([§3.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS1.SSS1); [§3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1); [§3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS4))
34: 
35: This creates a substantive representation issue: a fluent summary must not turn reconstructed holdings into certain dated purchase decisions or estimated profiles into confirmed preferences. Because some early-dated buys are reconstructed using end-of-release balances, a timestamp-before-cutoff filter alone does not prove contemporaneous observability. This is an **inferred point-in-time validity concern**, not a measured leakage effect. Equal treatment across representations is necessary for comparison, but does not by itself establish historical authenticity. ([Construction basis, §3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1))
36: 
37: ### The published benchmark predicts new-to-user acquisitions
38: 
39: At recommendation time `t`, the formal target ranks assets from the available set excluding those the customer **bought before t**. Training uses past prices and transactions, with a binary acquisition matrix rather than graded spending/frequency ratings. The authors evaluate **61 time points**, beginning **1 August 2019**, described as “spaced two weeks apart”; they do not enumerate the complete schedule. Each point uses prior history and **six months of future acquisitions**. Assets purchased in both training and test contribute only to training. Customers must be active in both periods, and assets must have prices throughout the test period, aligning the population for purchase and profitability metrics. This is neither a random 80/20 protocol nor an unrestricted repeat-purchase task. ([§5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS1); [§5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1))
40: 
41: The stated candidate set is the available universe minus previously purchased assets, subject to test-pricing eligibility. The text does **not** establish a restriction to the 321 globally traded assets, a sampled-negative protocol, or exact per-window candidate counts. **nDCG@10** measures future-acquisition relevance. **ROI@10** is reported as the monthly average return of an equally weighted top-ten portfolio over the six-month horizon; **0.0259 means 2.59% monthly**, not a 2.59% six-month total. The original workshop text does not give the exact monthly conversion equation. Table 2 averages over evaluation time points; detailed within-window weights are unspecified. ([§§5.1–5.2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))
42: 
43: ### Eleven methods provide substantial non-LLM benchmarks
44: 
45: The random baseline is accompanied by three price-based ROI regressors: **random forest, linear regression and LightGBM**, using indicators such as average price, past ROI, volatility, MACD, momentum, rate of change, RSI, detrended price oscillator, ROI/volatility and previous-period extrema. Transaction methods are **popularity**, **LightGCN**, **Apriori association-rule mining (ARM)**, **matrix factorization (MF)** and **user-based kNN**. Popularity is described as number of prior purchases; the paper does not fully reconcile event-count popularity with binary acquisition preprocessing. Two hybrids use recommender outputs as features: **LightGBM regression** for profitability and **LambdaMART/Hybrid-nDCG** for ranking. Neither hybrid uses generated text. All algorithms' hyperparameters are selected by **six-month ROI at 1 April 2019, 1 October 2019 and 31 January 2020**, including the model with an nDCG training objective. ([§5.2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS3))
46: 
47: The complete published Table 2 is reproduced below. ROI retains the paper's decimal monthly scale; market/customer rows are references, not additional algorithms. ([§5.3/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2))
48: 
49: | Family | Algorithm/reference | nDCG@10 | Monthly ROI@10 |
50: |---|---|---:|---:|
51: | None | Random | 0.0106 | 0.0071 |
52: | Prices | Random forest | 0.0237 | 0.0259 |
53: | Prices | Linear regression | 0.0215 | 0.0249 |
54: | Prices | LightGBM | 0.0221 | 0.0225 |
55: | Transactions | Popularity | 0.2710 | 0.0006 |
56: | Transactions | LightGCN | **0.3404** | 0.0004 |
57: | Transactions | ARM | 0.2556 | 0.0007 |
58: | Transactions | MF | 0.1780 | 0.0038 |
59: | Transactions | User-based kNN | 0.1599 | 0.0119 |
60: | Hybrid | Hybrid-nDCG | 0.2313 | 0.0063 |
61: | Hybrid | Hybrid-regression | 0.0261 | 0.0132 |
62: | Reference | Market average | — | 0.0079 |
63: | Reference | Customer average | — | 0.0018 |
64: 
65: **Only LightGCN exceeds popularity on nDCG in this comparison.** Its advantage is 0.0694 absolute, approximately 25.6% relative, calculated from the table, not an LLM effect or a significance claim. The best price model on ROI is poor at predicting purchases. The authors' conclusion explicitly separates profitable-asset discovery from predicting customer investments. Popularity therefore deserves serious attention in subsequent benchmark discussions, while the scores themselves are contextual published aggregates, not target scores for a sparse cohort. ([Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2); [§6](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S6))
66: 
67: ### Sparsity motivation is stronger than sparse-user effect evidence
68: 
69: The paper states that **over 50% of users have three or fewer transactions over 2018–2022**. That is full-period total activity, not pre-cutoff Buy counts or distinct purchased assets. It reports no sparse-specific nDCG, summary arm, confidence intervals or significance tests for Table 2. Six-month windows at approximately fortnightly origins overlap, and the listed ROI-tuning dates are not all earlier than the first test origin. Exact date lists, seeds, per-window populations, tuning grids and nested chronological validation are not established in the inspected text. These are reproducibility/interpretation limits, not proof of a quantified implementation error. A single institution, concentrated asset popularity and one market period also bound transfer. ([§3.3.2/Fig.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS2); [§5.2–5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))
70: 
71: ### Task1 supplies local context without defining the experimental cohort
72: 
73: The existing local inspection reports **388,048 transaction data rows**, **29,090 customers**, **320 traded ISINs**, **806 metadata ISINs**, and **807 price-series ISINs**. Table 1's transaction/traded-asset counts are **388,049 / 321**. The paper itself also mixes 806 in Table 1 and 807 in §3.2. One header makes the local CSV-record total 388,049, but that arithmetic does **not establish why the paper differs**. Local transaction dates extend to **30 November 2022**, whereas the institutional collection metadata ends **29 November**; prices locally end on 29 November. These distinctions remain unresolved rather than silently harmonized. ([Task1 inventory, “Customers, assets and transactions”](dataset_inventory.md#customers-assets-and-transactions); [Task1 date checks](data_quality_analysis.md#dates-and-numeric-checks); [paper Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1); [institutional dataset record](https://researchdata.gla.ac.uk/1658/))
74: 
75: Task1's full-release median is **three total events and two Buy events**; **21,237 customers (73.00%)** have 1–3 Buys, **23,663 (81.34%)** have 1–5, and **25,736 (88.47%)** have 1–10. These overlapping bands are descriptive only. Moreover, **360** customers in the 1–5 Buy band have more than ten total events, so purchase-sparse does not necessarily mean sparse buy/sell input. Task1's proposed 1–5 pre-cutoff Buy band remains provisional. It cannot be populated by reusing whole-release counts. ([Task1 sparse-user analysis](sparse_user_analysis.md))
76: 
77: Information equivalence must also account for measured metadata quality: among **836 asset metadata rows**, sector is blank in **388** and industry in **439**; **three ISIN/date keys** have conflicting records. Transaction IDs alone repeat, while `(customerID, transactionID)` is unique in the measured release. **12,501 customer-profile rows** have questionnaire dates later than their own snapshot timestamps. These are row/key-level observations, not counts of sparse users. They matter because summary generation can hide missingness, conflate records or add unsupported preference interpretations; the structured comparator should receive the same permitted, time-valid fields. ([Task1 data-quality analysis, missing values, key duplication and timing](data_quality_analysis.md))
78: 
79: ## FLARKO supplies same-dataset LLM evidence, not a summary comparison
80: 
81: Spadea and Seneviratne's FLARKO constructs a **personal knowledge graph** with ISIN, buy/sell type, value and timestamp, and a **market knowledge graph** with price summaries and asset category/sector/industry. Both are triples serialized as **JSON-LD**, capped jointly at **5,000 triples**. Ten-week price summaries are numeric aggregations, not LLM-written transaction narratives. Events and completed price-summary periods precede the recommendation date. Qwen3 models receive these graphs and generate three ISINs for the next six months. **KTO** labels desirable recommendations using the intersection of an actual purchase within **180 days** and a positive asset return. The method therefore changes representation, ranking model and behavioral/profitability supervision together. ([arXiv v1, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S3))
82: 
83: The study uses FAR-Trans training data from **2 January 2018–30 November 2021**, with prompts every four weeks during **1 August 2019–1 June 2021**. Test data span **1 December 2021–29 November 2022**, with prompts every two weeks during **1 December 2021–2 June 2022** and 180-day outcome buffers. Qwen3 sizes are **0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and 8B**; centralized training uses three epochs, while simulated federated experiments use twenty clients and omit 8B for compute reasons. The **23,784 balanced labeled examples** are training examples, not a reported number of evaluated investors. The conventional baselines include random, price regressors and transaction-based popularity/CF/ARM methods. ([§6.1–6.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6))
84: 
85: Evaluation uses **Pref@3, Prof@3 and Comb@3**, described as Hits@3 against purchased, profitable and intersection sets. No nDCG@10 is reported. Table 2 gives **0.6B/PKG Pref@3 0.4439 ± 0.0355**, compared with **0.6B/Combined 0.0354 ± 0.0131**. The highest centralized preference score is **1.7B/MKG 0.5341 ± 0.0532**; highest profitability score is **4B/Combined 0.6400 ± 0.0554**; highest combined score is **1.7B/Nothing 0.3718 ± 0.0547**. These maxima belong to different configurations. The ± values are the caption's **standard errors of proportions**, not confidence intervals or across-seed standard deviations. ([§6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS3); [§7.1/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2))
86: 
87: The paper's broad conclusion that combining personal and market graphs yields the strongest results needs qualification: **Combined is below PKG on Pref@3 and Comb@3 for every centralized size**, and the best Comb@3 uses no explicit graph context. Section 7.1 acknowledges combined-context degradation. Section 7.3 compares selected best configurations with baselines and reports advantages on preference/joint hits, but exact graphical baseline differences were not digitized in the evidence notes. Nothing here shows that natural-language summaries outperform matched structured histories. ([§7.1–7.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7); [§8](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S8))
88: 
89: FLARKO is the **nearest application prior work**, but it has no pre-cutoff sparse-cohort analysis. PKG/MKG/Nothing ablations change information, and the text does not fully establish identical users/candidate lists across ablations, exact hit-rate denominators, repeat-purchase policy or invalid/duplicate-ISIN handling. These are verification gaps, not evidence that cohorts definitely changed. Its original v1 main text and local PDF were read during the evidence research; the ICAIF publication metadata is verified separately, while the final publisher text was blocked. ([§§6–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6); [ACM-deposited metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3768292.3770399))
90: 
91: ## Language-profile studies expose benefits and information loss
92: 
93: ### UPR supports editable review profiles, with competitive rather than superior ranking
94: 
95: Ramos, Rahmani, Wang, Fu and Lipani's **User Profile Recommendation (UPR)** extracts sentiment-bearing features from reviews, ranks them using rating-derived utility, coverage and significance, and prompts Llama2-7B or Mistral-7B to write a first-person profile. Defaults select **five features**, **five reviews per feature** and a **200-token** profile. A separately fine-tuned **GPT-2** predicts a rating from the profile and candidate item title. The generated profile is thus a compact, editable representation of explicit review sentiment, not a faithful serialization of transaction IDs, amounts and dates. ([ACL published PDF, §§3.2–3.4, 4.4; Appendix A](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
96: 
97: Amazon Movies and TV contains **4,811 users, 5,459 items and 288,693 records**; TripAdvisor contains **9,765 users, 6,280 items and 320,023 records**. The **8:1:1** split requires every user/item to appear in every split and at least **five training reviews per user**; no global chronological cutoff is established. RMSE/MAE evaluate ratings; MAP and nDCG@10 use **only explicitly rated test items in condensed lists**. Consequently, values near 0.94 cannot be compared with catalog-wide FAR-Trans purchase nDCG. ([§4.1/Table 1; §4.2, p.13975](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
98: 
99: Table 2 reports the following selected results. They are descriptive comparisons without a supplied equivalence test or uncertainty intervals for these pairs. ([Table 2, p.13977](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
100: 
101: | Model | Amazon RMSE | Amazon nDCG@10 | TripAdvisor RMSE | TripAdvisor nDCG@10 |
102: |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
103: | MF | 0.925 | **0.941** | 0.786 | **0.960** |
104: | UPR (Llama2) | 0.944 | 0.938 | 0.804 | 0.955 |
105: | UPR (Mistral) | 0.941 | 0.940 | 0.804 | 0.952 |
106: 
107: Profile quality was assessed by **five master's-student annotators**, fifty profiles per domain; relevance satisfaction was **90%/87%** for Amazon/TripAdvisor. An editing experiment with **200 users** and lists of **100 feature-matching plus 100 other items** found higher target-feature Coverage@10 after positive profile edits. This supports readability and steering, not future-purchase accuracy or financial utility. The authors also report hallucinated/inferred content, review dependence, loss of rare preferences and difficulties with negative preferences. ([§5.3/Table 3, §5.4; §§6–8; Appendix A.5–A.6](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
108: 
109: UPR belongs in the five-paper set because it concretely demonstrates the profile pipeline and its trade-offs. Its CF comparisons change architecture and available semantics, while the editing test intentionally adds preferences. Neither isolates the encoding of the same sparse history. Warm-start review selection and feature-count ablations are not pre-cutoff financial sparsity tests. ([§§3–5](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
110: 
111: ### LangPTune is the nearest methodological precedent and a necessary counterexample
112: 
113: The verified CIKM publication is **LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation** by Gao, Zhou, Dai and Joachims. The experimental text read is the local **`2410.18870v2.pdf`**, titled **End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles**, dated **12 February 2025**. The initial preprint was submitted 24 October 2024; CIKM publication metadata dates to 10 November 2025. These are linked versions of the work, but final-table equivalence remains unchecked. ([Publication metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3746252.3761369); [official accepted papers](https://cikm2025.org/program/accepted-papers); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18870))
114: 
115: In v2, a **Gemma-2B-it or Llama-3-8B-Instruct** encoder generates a natural-language profile from historical item metadata and reviews. An **Mxbai embedding decoder** scores the profile against candidate metadata by inner product. **RLSO** optimizes the generator using downstream ranking rewards, while **contrastive learning (CL/InfoNCE)** trains the decoder; full LangPTune alternates both. This is task-optimized profile generation, not simply applying a fixed zero-shot summarizer. The variants freeze both components (-0), train only the decoder (-CL), or train only the generator (-RLSO). ([v2 §§3.1–3.2, 4.2–4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S3))
116: 
117: Amazon Movie-TV and Books examples contain **four distinct historical items and one distinct future item**, after filtering sessions/items with fewer than five interactions and overly long metadata/histories. Movie-TV has **14,698/1,392/1,392** train/validation/test sessions and **10,533 items**; Books has **4,404/361/361** sessions and **4,819 items**. Metrics are **Recall@20, MRR@20 and NDCG@20**. The short inputs are relevant to the RQ, but are not naturally sparse FAR-Trans cohorts selected before a shared calendar cutoff. Baseline access to validation/test history items, permitted by footnote 1, further differs from a simple globally chronological split; that is not by itself evidence of future-target leakage. ([v2 §4.1/Table 1; §4.2/footnote 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T1))
118: 
119: Joint training improves several language-profile baselines: Llama/Movie-TV NDCG@20 increases from **0.0231** (-0) to **0.0494** (full); Gemma/Books increases from **0.1743** to **0.2736**. The reported **113.9%** and **57.0%** relative gains compare optimized with zero-shot profile pipelines, **not summaries with structured histories**. Full LangPTune is not uniformly best against conventional models: Movie-TV **0.0494** is below LightGCN **0.0525** and MCL **0.0563**, whereas Books **0.2736** exceeds LightGCN **0.2586**. ([v2 Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T2))
120: 
121: The most relevant comparison bypasses profile generation: **NoProfile-0** directly embeds the historical item-metadata list with pretrained Mxbai; **NoProfile-CL** trains this direct-input decoder with InfoNCE. Table 4 gives the following **Movie-TV/Llama** results. ([v2 §4.5.1/Table 4, p.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4))
122: 
123: | Pipeline | Maximum profile tokens | Recall@20 | MRR@20 | NDCG@20 |
124: |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
125: | LangPTune | 64 | 0.0604 | 0.0201 | 0.0319 |
126: | LangPTune | 128 | 0.0901 | 0.0313 | 0.0444 |
127: | LangPTune | 256 | 0.0929 | 0.0352 | 0.0482 |
128: | LangPTune | 512 | 0.0970 | 0.0358 | 0.0494 |
129: | NoProfile-0 | — | 0.0760 | 0.0261 | 0.0372 |
130: | **NoProfile-CL** | — | **0.1012** | **0.0408** | **0.0543** |
131: 
132: **The best direct-history comparator exceeds the 512-token profile by 0.0049 NDCG@20.** Equivalently, the profile is approximately 9.0% below NoProfile-CL, arithmetic derived from the table; this pair has no reported significance marker. The authors explicitly discuss the language-profile information bottleneck. A limited fixed-decoder comparison also exists: **NoProfile-0 0.0372**, **LangPTune-0 0.0231**, and **LangPTune-RLSO 0.0377** use the pretrained decoder on Movie-TV. This is relevant partial control evidence and should not be dismissed, but reviews, formatting/truncation parity and significance of these exact contrasts remain unresolved. Full LangPTune versus NoProfile-CL instead uses separately trained decoder weights and different training settings. ([v2 Tables 2/4, §§4.2.1, 4.5.1; Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2))
133: 
134: Two other distinctions prevent overstatement. Reducing **global training-set size from 100% to 0.1%** is not a per-user sparsity experiment. The human interpretability test finds **58.89%** binary next-movie choice accuracy for trained profiles versus **57.11%** raw history and **54.67%** zero-shot profiles, with trained-versus-raw **p=0.624** and trained-versus-zero-shot **p=0.201**. Those nonsignificant comparisons and shorter reading times concern a readability/usefulness trade-off, not proof of superior ranking or faithful transaction summaries. ([v2 §4.5.2/Fig.4; §4.6/Tables 5–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.SS6))
135: 
136: ## Financial evaluation bounds the meaning of an eventual result
137: 
138: ### Investors Are (Not) Always Right separates predicting purchases from earning returns
139: 
140: Sanz-Cruzado, McCreadie, Droukas, Macdonald and Ounis compare transaction-based and customer-independent profitability metrics theoretically and empirically. Theorem 5.6 establishes **zero correlation over all possible valid user–ranking pairs at a fixed time/horizon**, under its assumptions. The authors use “independence,” but zero covariance alone is not general statistical independence; the safe substantive conclusion is **no guaranteed positive relationship**, not a universal law about actual investors. ([TOIS §5.3, Theorem 5.6](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-5-3))
141: 
142: The empirical study uses FAR-Trans and **twelve algorithms**, adding **customer profile similarity (CPS)** to the original eleven-method inventory. The main protocol has **61 temporal variants**, a six-month horizon, binary novel-acquisition relevance and test-activity/pricing filters. Hyperparameters are again selected for six-month ROI at the three dates described above. The article states origins from **1 August 2019 to end-November 2021**, spaced two weeks apart; those statements do not yield an unambiguous literal 61-origin schedule. A complete date list remains a reproduction question. CPS also uses demographic information that the article's Data Statement says could not be publicly shared. ([§6.1–6.3](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6); [Data Statement](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-13))
143: 
144: Unlike the workshop paper, this article supplies explicit metric equations: binary purchase gain with logarithmic rank discount, an equally weighted top-k portfolio, and monthly conversion **`(1 + ROI)^(30 / horizon_days) − 1`**. The reported pooled correlation between **nDCG@10 and monthly ROI@10 is −0.13**, over approximately **1.5 million user × algorithm × temporal-variant values**, with authors reporting **p < 0.05**. This is not a correlation over only twelve model means. Repeated users and overlapping horizons mean that the pooled count should not be treated automatically as independent observations; the literature notes did not recalculate the uncertainty. ([§6.2/Eqs.7–12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6-2); [§7/Fig.4, p.51:23](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))
145: 
146: Table 5 repeats shared FAR-Trans baseline values, including **LightGCN 0.3404 nDCG / 0.0004 monthly ROI**, **popularity 0.2710 / 0.0006**, and **random forest 0.0237 / 0.0259**. CPS gives **0.2722 / 0.0026**. These are useful metric contrasts, not a second independent demonstration of representation gains. The article's synthetic effective-investor experiment changes the pooled correlation to **+0.13**; date-specific correlations vary approximately **−0.65 to +0.4**. Thus a universally negative empirical relation is also unsupported. ([§8.1/Table 5](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#tab5); [§9.2/Fig.7](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-9-2); [§10/Fig.8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-10))
147: 
148: Limitations include one institution, partial portfolios, omitted dividend/coupon income, equal-allocation/customer-independent profitability and simplified common investment horizons. The authors explicitly say abandoning transaction-based evaluation is premature. For this RQ, improved nDCG@10 would mean **better ranking of future observed purchases**, not necessarily higher profits, suitability, risk reduction or welfare. The article contains no LLM-summary experiment or sparse-specific representation result. ([§12 and limitations](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-12))
149: 
150: ### Conv-FinRe is an investigated alternative with a different target
151: 
152: **Conv-FinRe: A Conversational and Longitudinal Benchmark for Utility-Grounded Financial Recommendation** is verified as a **SIGIR 2026** publication. Experimental claims here use **arXiv v2**, a pre-camera-ready version. The publisher-deposited record has **thirteen authors**, while the arXiv version has **fourteen**, including **Rosie Guo** rather than the publication's **Yuqing Guo**, and **Xue Liu**, absent from the publication metadata. Their identities/reasons for the differences are not inferred; both full lists appear in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md#6-conv-finre--investigated-alternative). ([Publisher-deposited record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3805712.3808658); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16990))
153: 
154: This benchmark combines real market prices with **ten human participants' simulator decisions**, not FAR-Trans brokerage purchases. Ten stocks and **23 steps per user** yield **230 prefix-conditioned instances**, **270 unique turns** and **3,450 prefix-expanded turns**. Onboarding and later dialogues are generated from profiles and decision trajectories, rather than collected natural human-advisor conversations. Models rerank the fixed stock set using profile/history, market and advisor information. Utility combines standardized seven-day return with individual volatility/drawdown penalties, whose parameters are fitted over each participant's **full longitudinal trajectory**. ([v2 §§3.1–3.3/Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3))
155: 
156: Metrics include **utility-gain uNDCG over the full candidate set**, choice MRR/HR@1/HR@3 and Kendall τ against advisor rankings. Table 4 reports **Llama-3.3-70B uNDCG 0.97 ± 0.00**, while the finance-specific **XuanYuan3** has **MRR 0.65 ± 0.03** and **HR@1 0.54 ± 0.03**. The inspected caption/text does not clearly identify the ± estimator, so these are retained as reported uncertainty, not relabeled standard errors. History/no-history results are model-dependent: some improve, some barely change, and some lose utility alignment. Removing history changes information; it is not a summary-versus-structured contrast. ([v2 §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS4); [Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.T4); [§4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.SS3))
157: 
158: The small repeated-prefix sample, generated dialogue and retrospective utility calibration limit transfer. Full-trajectory fitting raises a point-in-time question if adapted to prospective prediction, without establishing a measured leakage effect in this diagnostic benchmark. The signed-utility equations do not document a nonnegative gain transformation, so conventional binary-nDCG bounds cannot be assumed; **0.97 is not comparable with FAR-Trans's 0.3404**. This paper is retained as adjacent evaluation context and excluded from the core five because Investors supplies more direct FAR-Trans metric evidence, while LangPTune better addresses the representation question. ([v2 §§3.2–3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS2); [§5](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S5))
159: 
160: ## The preparation supports a bounded, two-sided research gap
161: 
162: **Among the studies inspected, we did not find a same-information comparison of LLM-generated transaction-history summaries versus structured-history features for a pre-cutoff sparse FAR-Trans cohort, evaluated on future-purchase nDCG@10 under matched users, candidates and downstream ranking conditions.** LangPTune is the closest methodological precedent because it tests bypassing the profile generator, including frozen-decoder variants; FLARKO is closest in dataset/application. Neither establishes the requested financial effect. UPR's lower nDCG than MF, LangPTune's direct-history advantage and FLARKO's mixed context results make a negative or null outcome scientifically informative. No expected effect size can be transferred across their different relevance definitions, cutoffs and candidate sets. ([LangPTune v2 Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FLARKO Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2); [UPR Table 2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))
163: 
164: The remaining preparation task is to clarify the permitted comparison once the class protocol is available: historical information, sparse counting unit, new versus repeat purchases, candidate availability and what “fixed ranker” means. [research_gap.md](research_gap.md) records these as **pending controls**, not an approved experiment or an invented official split.
165: 
166: ## Source-linked references
167: 
168: 1. **Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Nikolaos Droukas, and Richard McCreadie. 2024.** *FAR-Trans: An Investment Dataset for Financial Asset Recommendation.* IJCAI-24 Workshop on Recommender Systems in Finance (Fin-RecSys). [Original v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1); [official workshop program](https://sites.google.com/view/fin-recsys2024/program). **arXiv DOI:** [10.48550/arXiv.2407.08692](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2407.08692), not a verified proceedings DOI.
169: 2. **Fernando Spadea and Oshani Seneviratne. 2025.** *Aligning Language Models with Investor and Market Behavior for Financial Recommendations.* Proceedings of the 6th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '25), 509–517. **Publication DOI:** [10.1145/3768292.3770399](https://doi.org/10.1145/3768292.3770399). [Original v1 evidence](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1); [publication metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3768292.3770399).
170: 3. **Jerome Ramos, Hossein A. Rahmani, Xi Wang, Xiao Fu, and Aldo Lipani. 2024.** *Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles.* Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 13971–13984. **Publication DOI:** [10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.753](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.753). [Official record](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753/); [published full text](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf).
171: 4. **Zhaolin Gao, Joyce Zhou, Yijia Dai, and Thorsten Joachims. 2025.** *LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation.* Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '25), 707–717. **Publication DOI:** [10.1145/3746252.3761369](https://doi.org/10.1145/3746252.3761369). [Publication metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3746252.3761369). Experimental evidence: same authors, *End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles*, [arXiv:2410.18870v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2), 12 February 2025; separate **arXiv DOI:** [10.48550/arXiv.2410.18870](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2410.18870).
172: 5. **Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Richard McCreadie, Nikolaos Droukas, Craig Macdonald, and Iadh Ounis. 2026.** *Investors Are (Not) Always Right: A Comparison of Transaction-Based and Profitability-Based Metrics for Financial Asset Recommendations.* ACM Transactions on Information Systems 44(2), Article 51, 56 pages. **Publication DOI:** [10.1145/3780097](https://doi.org/10.1145/3780097). [Published HTML](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097); [published repository PDF](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/373432/2/373432.pdf).
173: 6. **Yan Wang, Yi Han, Lingfei Qian, Yueru He, Xueqing Peng, Dongji Feng, Zhuohan Xie, Vincent Jim Zhang, Yuqing Guo, Fengran Mo, Jimin Huang, Yankai Chen, and Jian-Yun Nie. 2026.** *Conv-FinRe: A Conversational and Longitudinal Benchmark for Utility-Grounded Financial Recommendation.* Proceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '26), 3448–3455. **Publication DOI:** [10.1145/3805712.3808658](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805712.3808658). This list is from [publisher-deposited metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3805712.3808658); experimental evidence is [arXiv v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2), with a different author list documented separately.

# Literature clarifies the sparse-history summary question

**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
**Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University  
**Scope:** Task2 literature preparation notes.

**Research question:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?

**The inspected evidence does not establish the answer to this exact question.** FAR-Trans supplies the financial dataset and purchase-ranking benchmark; FLARKO demonstrates LLM recommendation on that dataset; UPR and LangPTune supply language-profile methods. However, LangPTune's closest direct-history comparison favors **NoProfile-CL (NDCG@20 0.0543) over the 512-token profile (0.0494)** on Movie-TV. The financial-evaluation literature also shows why purchase prediction must be distinguished from profitability. Together, these results motivate a controlled, two-sided investigation rather than a claim that summaries already improve sparse-investor recommendations. All LangPTune experimental claims below refer to the **February 2025 arXiv v2 manuscript**, not an independently checked final CIKM text. ([LangPTune v2, §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FAR-Trans, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5); [Investors, §§7–8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

The five core studies are selected for complementary relevance. **FAR-Trans** is the foundation; **LangPTune** is the nearest methodological prior work among those inspected; **FLARKO** is the nearest same-dataset LLM application; **UPR** establishes the review-to-profile and editability rationale; **Investors Are (Not) Always Right** provides directly relevant metric interpretation. **Conv-FinRe was also investigated**, but remains an optional contextual source because its ten-participant conversational simulation and utility-based relevance are less directly matched to this RQ. # Literature clarifies the sparse-history summary question

**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
**Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University  
**Scope:** Task2 literature preparation notes.

**Research question:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?

**The inspected evidence does not establish the answer to this exact question.** FAR-Trans supplies the financial dataset and purchase-ranking benchmark; FLARKO demonstrates LLM recommendation on that dataset; UPR and LangPTune supply language-profile methods. However, LangPTune's closest direct-history comparison favors **NoProfile-CL (NDCG@20 0.0543) over the 512-token profile (0.0494)** on Movie-TV. The financial-evaluation literature also shows why purchase prediction must be distinguished from profitability. Together, these results motivate a controlled, two-sided investigation rather than a claim that summaries already improve sparse-investor recommendations. All LangPTune experimental claims below refer to the **February 2025 arXiv v2 manuscript**, not an independently checked final CIKM text. ([LangPTune v2, §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FAR-Trans, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5); [Investors, §§7–8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

This synthesis uses all five evidence-note files in `research_notes/Sparse financial recommendation literature/` and the existing Task1 measurements. Source reading/access is inherited from those documented research records; this writing pass read the notes rather than reopening academic full texts. AI assistance: OpenCode, `openai/gpt-6-astra`. The user reports personally verifying **transaction7590224 and asset metadata**; personal paper verification remains pending. Detailed bibliographies, access boundaries and claim locators are in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md); the bounded gap and pending controls are in [research_gap.md](research_gap.md).

## Five studies cover the dataset, method and evaluation

The five core studies are selected for complementary relevance. **FAR-Trans** is the foundation; **LangPTune** is the nearest methodological prior work among those inspected; **FLARKO** is the nearest same-dataset LLM application; **UPR** establishes the review-to-profile and editability rationale; **Investors Are (Not) Always Right** provides directly relevant metric interpretation. **Conv-FinRe was also investigated**, but remains an optional contextual source because its ten-participant conversational simulation and utility-based relevance are less directly matched to this RQ. This is a relevance judgment within six inspected studies, not an exhaustive ranking of the literature.

### Professor-facing comparison table

| Study (authors, year, venue) | Problem/method | Data/evaluation | Limitation/link to RQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FAR-Trans: An Investment Dataset for Financial Asset Recommendation** — Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Nikolaos Droukas, Richard McCreadie (2024), IJCAI-24 **Fin-RecSys workshop** | Public financial recommendation dataset; 11 random, price, transaction and hybrid methods; binary acquisition history. | FAR-Trans; 61 temporal variants, six-month future novel acquisitions; nDCG@10 and monthly ROI@10. LightGCN **0.3404**, popularity **0.2710** nDCG@10. | Foundational dataset/protocol, not an LLM or sparse-cohort comparison. Reconstructed holdings complicate point-in-time interpretation; published aggregates are not class/sparse results. [§§3, 5; Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2) |
| **Aligning Language Models with Investor and Market Behavior for Financial Recommendations** — Fernando Spadea, Oshani Seneviratne (2025), **ICAIF '25**; FLARKO | Qwen3 receives personal/market KGs serialized as JSON-LD; KTO aligns recommendations with future purchases and positive returns; centralized/federated variants. | FAR-Trans; 180-day outcomes; Pref@3, Prof@3, Comb@3. Centralized best Comb@3 **0.3718 ± 0.0547**, 1.7B/**Nothing** context. | Same dataset and LLMs, but graph inputs are not generated narrative histories; no nDCG@10 or sparse-user result. Context removal changes information. Results read in arXiv v1; publication metadata separately verified. [§§3–7; Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2) |
| **Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles** — Jerome Ramos, Hossein A. Rahmani, Xi Wang, Xiao Fu, Aldo Lipani (2024), **ACL, Volume 1: Long Papers**; UPR | Generate first-person profiles from selected review features using Llama2/Mistral; GPT-2 predicts ratings from profile and item title; profile edits steer recommendations. | Amazon Movies and TV / TripAdvisor; ≥5 training reviews/user; RMSE, MAE, MAP and **condensed-list** nDCG@10. Best UPR nDCG **0.940 / 0.955**, MF **0.941 / 0.960**. | Feasible, editable profiles; no ranking superiority over MF here. Review-rich warm-start ratings differ from sparse financial purchase prediction; model and information differ across baselines. [§§3–5; Table 2, p.13977](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf) |
| **LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation** — Zhaolin Gao, Joyce Zhou, Yijia Dai, Thorsten Joachims (2025), **CIKM '25** | Jointly optimize LLM profile generator with RLSO and Mxbai embedding ranker with contrastive learning; compare direct-history NoProfile variants. | **Evidence: arXiv v2, differently titled** *End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles*. Amazon Movie-TV/Books; four history items → one future item; Recall/MRR/NDCG@20. Movie-TV NoProfile-CL **0.0543 > 0.0494** full 512-token profile. | Closest method/control evidence; compression can hurt. No FAR-Trans or pre-cutoff sparse cohort; review parity unresolved; separately trained rankers differ. Final CIKM tables not checked. [v2 §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4) |
| **Investors Are (Not) Always Right: A Comparison of Transaction-Based and Profitability-Based Metrics for Financial Asset Recommendations** — Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Richard McCreadie, Nikolaos Droukas, Craig Macdonald, Iadh Ounis (2026), **ACM TOIS 44(2), Article 51** | Formal metric analysis and 12-algorithm empirical comparison; tests whether purchase relevance substitutes for profitability. | FAR-Trans; 61 temporal variants, main six-month horizon; pooled nDCG@10/monthly ROI@10 correlation **−0.13**, approximately 1.5 million user × algorithm × date observations. | Supports purchase/return distinction, not summaries. No representation arm or sparse subgroup. Shared FAR-Trans baseline values are not an independent replication of summary gains. [§§6–8; Fig.4/Table 5](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7) |

## FAR-Trans anchors the task but leaves sparse-summary effects unmeasured

### Dataset construction matters to what a summary can truthfully say

Sanz-Cruzado, Droukas and McCreadie describe investment opportunities available to Greek investors through one large European financial institution, including stocks, bonds, mutual funds, asset prices, anonymized customers and buy/sell logs from January 2018 to November 2022. Table 1 reports **29,090 customers, 806 unique assets, 321 assets with investments, 703,303 price points, 388,049 transactions, 228,913 acquisitions and 159,136 sales**. The parenthetical “unique” transaction/acquisition counts in that table do not have a sufficiently explicit deduplication key to relabel them as distinct user–item pairs. Their qualified novelty claim concerns a public FAR dataset containing **both prices and investment transactions**, not the absence of all earlier public financial recommendation data. ([§§2.2–3/Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1))

The released events are **processed and partly reconstructed**, not all untouched observed purchases. The authors remove transactions lacking customer IDs, adjust shares for stock splits and insert cash-in-lieu sales for fractional shares after reverse splits. When end-2022 balances imply sales from pre-existing holdings, they recreate the missing buys at the earliest available price date, usually 2 January 2018. Transactions outside a price series are moved to its nearest covered date; remaining holdings can be closed when a price series ends; monetary values are estimated from adjusted shares and closing prices. Prices themselves are cleaned, euro-converted, split-adjusted and gap-filled. Customer risk/capacity can be estimated rather than questionnaire-observed. ([§3.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS1.SSS1); [§3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1); [§3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS4))

This creates a substantive representation issue: a fluent summary must not turn reconstructed holdings into certain dated purchase decisions or estimated profiles into confirmed preferences. Because some early-dated buys are reconstructed using end-of-release balances, a timestamp-before-cutoff filter alone does not prove contemporaneous observability. This is an **inferred point-in-time validity concern**, not a measured leakage effect. Equal treatment across representations is necessary for comparison, but does not by itself establish historical authenticity. ([Construction basis, §3.3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS1))

### The published benchmark predicts new-to-user acquisitions

At recommendation time `t`, the formal target ranks assets from the available set excluding those the customer **bought before t**. Training uses past prices and transactions, with a binary acquisition matrix rather than graded spending/frequency ratings. The authors evaluate **61 time points**, beginning **1 August 2019**, described as “spaced two weeks apart”; they do not enumerate the complete schedule. Each point uses prior history and **six months of future acquisitions**. Assets purchased in both training and test contribute only to training. Customers must be active in both periods, and assets must have prices throughout the test period, aligning the population for purchase and profitability metrics. This is neither a random 80/20 protocol nor an unrestricted repeat-purchase task. ([§5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS1); [§5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1))

The stated candidate set is the available universe minus previously purchased assets, subject to test-pricing eligibility. The text does **not** establish a restriction to the 321 globally traded assets, a sampled-negative protocol, or exact per-window candidate counts. **nDCG@10** measures future-acquisition relevance. **ROI@10** is reported as the monthly average return of an equally weighted top-ten portfolio over the six-month horizon; **0.0259 means 2.59% monthly**, not a 2.59% six-month total. The original workshop text does not give the exact monthly conversion equation. Table 2 averages over evaluation time points; detailed within-window weights are unspecified. ([§§5.1–5.2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))

### Eleven methods provide substantial non-LLM benchmarks

The random baseline is accompanied by three price-based ROI regressors: **random forest, linear regression and LightGBM**, using indicators such as average price, past ROI, volatility, MACD, momentum, rate of change, RSI, detrended price oscillator, ROI/volatility and previous-period extrema. Transaction methods are **popularity**, **LightGCN**, **Apriori association-rule mining (ARM)**, **matrix factorization (MF)** and **user-based kNN**. Popularity is described as number of prior purchases; the paper does not fully reconcile event-count popularity with binary acquisition preprocessing. Two hybrids use recommender outputs as features: **LightGBM regression** for profitability and **LambdaMART/Hybrid-nDCG** for ranking. Neither hybrid uses generated text. All algorithms' hyperparameters are selected by **six-month ROI at 1 April 2019, 1 October 2019 and 31 January 2020**, including the model with an nDCG training objective. ([§5.2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS3))

The complete published Table 2 is reproduced below. ROI retains the paper's decimal monthly scale; market/customer rows are references, not additional algorithms. ([§5.3/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2))

| Family | Algorithm/reference | nDCG@10 | Monthly ROI@10 |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| None | Random | 0.0106 | 0.0071 |
| Prices | Random forest | 0.0237 | 0.0259 |
| Prices | Linear regression | 0.0215 | 0.0249 |
| Prices | LightGBM | 0.0221 | 0.0225 |
| Transactions | Popularity | 0.2710 | 0.0006 |
| Transactions | LightGCN | **0.3404** | 0.0004 |
| Transactions | ARM | 0.2556 | 0.0007 |
| Transactions | MF | 0.1780 | 0.0038 |
| Transactions | User-based kNN | 0.1599 | 0.0119 |
| Hybrid | Hybrid-nDCG | 0.2313 | 0.0063 |
| Hybrid | Hybrid-regression | 0.0261 | 0.0132 |
| Reference | Market average | — | 0.0079 |
| Reference | Customer average | — | 0.0018 |

**Only LightGCN exceeds popularity on nDCG in this comparison.** Its advantage is 0.0694 absolute, approximately 25.6% relative, calculated from the table, not an LLM effect or a significance claim. The best price model on ROI is poor at predicting purchases. The authors' conclusion explicitly separates profitable-asset discovery from predicting customer investments. Popularity therefore deserves serious attention in subsequent benchmark discussions, while the scores themselves are contextual published aggregates, not target scores for a sparse cohort. ([Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.T2); [§6](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S6))

### Sparsity motivation is stronger than sparse-user effect evidence

The paper states that **over 50% of users have three or fewer transactions over 2018–2022**. That is full-period total activity, not pre-cutoff Buy counts or distinct purchased assets. It reports no sparse-specific nDCG, summary arm, confidence intervals or significance tests for Table 2. Six-month windows at approximately fortnightly origins overlap, and the listed ROI-tuning dates are not all earlier than the first test origin. Exact date lists, seeds, per-window populations, tuning grids and nested chronological validation are not established in the inspected text. These are reproducibility/interpretation limits, not proof of a quantified implementation error. A single institution, concentrated asset popularity and one market period also bound transfer. ([§3.3.2/Fig.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.SS3.SSS2); [§5.2–5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2))

### Task1 supplies local context without defining the experimental cohort

The existing local inspection reports **388,048 transaction data rows**, **29,090 customers**, **320 traded ISINs**, **806 metadata ISINs**, and **807 price-series ISINs**. Table 1's transaction/traded-asset counts are **388,049 / 321**. The paper itself also mixes 806 in Table 1 and 807 in §3.2. One header makes the local CSV-record total 388,049, but that arithmetic does **not establish why the paper differs**. Local transaction dates extend to **30 November 2022**, whereas the institutional collection metadata ends **29 November**; prices locally end on 29 November. These distinctions remain unresolved rather than silently harmonized. ([Task1 inventory, “Customers, assets and transactions”](dataset_inventory.md#customers-assets-and-transactions); [Task1 date checks](data_quality_analysis.md#dates-and-numeric-checks); [paper Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1); [institutional dataset record](https://researchdata.gla.ac.uk/1658/))

Task1's full-release median is **three total events and two Buy events**; **21,237 customers (73.00%)** have 1–3 Buys, **23,663 (81.34%)** have 1–5, and **25,736 (88.47%)** have 1–10. These overlapping bands are descriptive only. Moreover, **360** customers in the 1–5 Buy band have more than ten total events, so purchase-sparse does not necessarily mean sparse buy/sell input. Task1's proposed 1–5 pre-cutoff Buy band remains provisional. It cannot be populated by reusing whole-release counts. ([Task1 sparse-user analysis](sparse_user_analysis.md))

Information equivalence must also account for measured metadata quality: among **836 asset metadata rows**, sector is blank in **388** and industry in **439**; **three ISIN/date keys** have conflicting records. Transaction IDs alone repeat, while `(customerID, transactionID)` is unique in the measured release. **12,501 customer-profile rows** have questionnaire dates later than their own snapshot timestamps. These are row/key-level observations, not counts of sparse users. They matter because summary generation can hide missingness, conflate records or add unsupported preference interpretations; the structured comparator should receive the same permitted, time-valid fields. ([Task1 data-quality analysis, missing values, key duplication and timing](data_quality_analysis.md))

## FLARKO supplies same-dataset LLM evidence, not a summary comparison

Spadea and Seneviratne's FLARKO constructs a **personal knowledge graph** with ISIN, buy/sell type, value and timestamp, and a **market knowledge graph** with price summaries and asset category/sector/industry. Both are triples serialized as **JSON-LD**, capped jointly at **5,000 triples**. Ten-week price summaries are numeric aggregations, not LLM-written transaction narratives. Events and completed price-summary periods precede the recommendation date. Qwen3 models receive these graphs and generate three ISINs for the next six months. **KTO** labels desirable recommendations using the intersection of an actual purchase within **180 days** and a positive asset return. The method therefore changes representation, ranking model and behavioral/profitability supervision together. ([arXiv v1, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S3))

The study uses FAR-Trans training data from **2 January 2018–30 November 2021**, with prompts every four weeks during **1 August 2019–1 June 2021**. Test data span **1 December 2021–29 November 2022**, with prompts every two weeks during **1 December 2021–2 June 2022** and 180-day outcome buffers. Qwen3 sizes are **0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and 8B**; centralized training uses three epochs, while simulated federated experiments use twenty clients and omit 8B for compute reasons. The **23,784 balanced labeled examples** are training examples, not a reported number of evaluated investors. The conventional baselines include random, price regressors and transaction-based popularity/CF/ARM methods. ([§6.1–6.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6))

Evaluation uses **Pref@3, Prof@3 and Comb@3**, described as Hits@3 against purchased, profitable and intersection sets. No nDCG@10 is reported. Table 2 gives **0.6B/PKG Pref@3 0.4439 ± 0.0355**, compared with **0.6B/Combined 0.0354 ± 0.0131**. The highest centralized preference score is **1.7B/MKG 0.5341 ± 0.0532**; highest profitability score is **4B/Combined 0.6400 ± 0.0554**; highest combined score is **1.7B/Nothing 0.3718 ± 0.0547**. These maxima belong to different configurations. The ± values are the caption's **standard errors of proportions**, not confidence intervals or across-seed standard deviations. ([§6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS3); [§7.1/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2))

The paper's broad conclusion that combining personal and market graphs yields the strongest results needs qualification: **Combined is below PKG on Pref@3 and Comb@3 for every centralized size**, and the best Comb@3 uses no explicit graph context. Section 7.1 acknowledges combined-context degradation. Section 7.3 compares selected best configurations with baselines and reports advantages on preference/joint hits, but exact graphical baseline differences were not digitized in the evidence notes. Nothing here shows that natural-language summaries outperform matched structured histories. ([§7.1–7.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7); [§8](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S8))

FLARKO is the **nearest application prior work**, but it has no pre-cutoff sparse-cohort analysis. PKG/MKG/Nothing ablations change information, and the text does not fully establish identical users/candidate lists across ablations, exact hit-rate denominators, repeat-purchase policy or invalid/duplicate-ISIN handling. These are verification gaps, not evidence that cohorts definitely changed. Its original v1 main text and local PDF were read during the evidence research; the ICAIF publication metadata is verified separately, while the final publisher text was blocked. ([§§6–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6); [ACM-deposited metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3768292.3770399))

## Language-profile studies expose benefits and information loss

### UPR supports editable review profiles, with competitive rather than superior ranking

Ramos, Rahmani, Wang, Fu and Lipani's **User Profile Recommendation (UPR)** extracts sentiment-bearing features from reviews, ranks them using rating-derived utility, coverage and significance, and prompts Llama2-7B or Mistral-7B to write a first-person profile. Defaults select **five features**, **five reviews per feature** and a **200-token** profile. A separately fine-tuned **GPT-2** predicts a rating from the profile and candidate item title. The generated profile is thus a compact, editable representation of explicit review sentiment, not a faithful serialization of transaction IDs, amounts and dates. ([ACL published PDF, §§3.2–3.4, 4.4; Appendix A](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

Amazon Movies and TV contains **4,811 users, 5,459 items and 288,693 records**; TripAdvisor contains **9,765 users, 6,280 items and 320,023 records**. The **8:1:1** split requires every user/item to appear in every split and at least **five training reviews per user**; no global chronological cutoff is established. RMSE/MAE evaluate ratings; MAP and nDCG@10 use **only explicitly rated test items in condensed lists**. Consequently, values near 0.94 cannot be compared with catalog-wide FAR-Trans purchase nDCG. ([§4.1/Table 1; §4.2, p.13975](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

Table 2 reports the following selected results. They are descriptive comparisons without a supplied equivalence test or uncertainty intervals for these pairs. ([Table 2, p.13977](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

| Model | Amazon RMSE | Amazon nDCG@10 | TripAdvisor RMSE | TripAdvisor nDCG@10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MF | 0.925 | **0.941** | 0.786 | **0.960** |
| UPR (Llama2) | 0.944 | 0.938 | 0.804 | 0.955 |
| UPR (Mistral) | 0.941 | 0.940 | 0.804 | 0.952 |

Profile quality was assessed by **five master's-student annotators**, fifty profiles per domain; relevance satisfaction was **90%/87%** for Amazon/TripAdvisor. An editing experiment with **200 users** and lists of **100 feature-matching plus 100 other items** found higher target-feature Coverage@10 after positive profile edits. This supports readability and steering, not future-purchase accuracy or financial utility. The authors also report hallucinated/inferred content, review dependence, loss of rare preferences and difficulties with negative preferences. ([§5.3/Table 3, §5.4; §§6–8; Appendix A.5–A.6](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

UPR belongs in the five-paper set because it concretely demonstrates the profile pipeline and its trade-offs. Its CF comparisons change architecture and available semantics, while the editing test intentionally adds preferences. Neither isolates the encoding of the same sparse history. Warm-start review selection and feature-count ablations are not pre-cutoff financial sparsity tests. ([§§3–5](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

### LangPTune is the nearest methodological precedent and a necessary counterexample

The verified CIKM publication is **LangPTune: Optimizing Language-based User Profiles for Recommendation** by Gao, Zhou, Dai and Joachims. The experimental text read is the local **`2410.18870v2.pdf`**, titled **End-to-end Training for Recommendation with Language-based User Profiles**, dated **12 February 2025**. The initial preprint was submitted 24 October 2024; CIKM publication metadata dates to 10 November 2025. These are linked versions of the work, but final-table equivalence remains unchecked. ([Publication metadata](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3746252.3761369); [official accepted papers](https://cikm2025.org/program/accepted-papers); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18870))

In v2, a **Gemma-2B-it or Llama-3-8B-Instruct** encoder generates a natural-language profile from historical item metadata and reviews. An **Mxbai embedding decoder** scores the profile against candidate metadata by inner product. **RLSO** optimizes the generator using downstream ranking rewards, while **contrastive learning (CL/InfoNCE)** trains the decoder; full LangPTune alternates both. This is task-optimized profile generation, not simply applying a fixed zero-shot summarizer. The variants freeze both components (-0), train only the decoder (-CL), or train only the generator (-RLSO). ([v2 §§3.1–3.2, 4.2–4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S3))

Amazon Movie-TV and Books examples contain **four distinct historical items and one distinct future item**, after filtering sessions/items with fewer than five interactions and overly long metadata/histories. Movie-TV has **14,698/1,392/1,392** train/validation/test sessions and **10,533 items**; Books has **4,404/361/361** sessions and **4,819 items**. Metrics are **Recall@20, MRR@20 and NDCG@20**. The short inputs are relevant to the RQ, but are not naturally sparse FAR-Trans cohorts selected before a shared calendar cutoff. Baseline access to validation/test history items, permitted by footnote 1, further differs from a simple globally chronological split; that is not by itself evidence of future-target leakage. ([v2 §4.1/Table 1; §4.2/footnote 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T1))

Joint training improves several language-profile baselines: Llama/Movie-TV NDCG@20 increases from **0.0231** (-0) to **0.0494** (full); Gemma/Books increases from **0.1743** to **0.2736**. The reported **113.9%** and **57.0%** relative gains compare optimized with zero-shot profile pipelines, **not summaries with structured histories**. Full LangPTune is not uniformly best against conventional models: Movie-TV **0.0494** is below LightGCN **0.0525** and MCL **0.0563**, whereas Books **0.2736** exceeds LightGCN **0.2586**. ([v2 Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T2))

The most relevant comparison bypasses profile generation: **NoProfile-0** directly embeds the historical item-metadata list with pretrained Mxbai; **NoProfile-CL** trains this direct-input decoder with InfoNCE. Table 4 gives the following **Movie-TV/Llama** results. ([v2 §4.5.1/Table 4, p.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4))

| Pipeline | Maximum profile tokens | Recall@20 | MRR@20 | NDCG@20 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| LangPTune | 64 | 0.0604 | 0.0201 | 0.0319 |
| LangPTune | 128 | 0.0901 | 0.0313 | 0.0444 |
| LangPTune | 256 | 0.0929 | 0.0352 | 0.0482 |
| LangPTune | 512 | 0.0970 | 0.0358 | 0.0494 |
| NoProfile-0 | — | 0.0760 | 0.0261 | 0.0372 |
| **NoProfile-CL** | — | **0.1012** | **0.0408** | **0.0543** |

**The best direct-history comparator exceeds the 512-token profile by 0.0049 NDCG@20.** Equivalently, the profile is approximately 9.0% below NoProfile-CL, arithmetic derived from the table; this pair has no reported significance marker. The authors explicitly discuss the language-profile information bottleneck. A limited fixed-decoder comparison also exists: **NoProfile-0 0.0372**, **LangPTune-0 0.0231**, and **LangPTune-RLSO 0.0377** use the pretrained decoder on Movie-TV. This is relevant partial control evidence and should not be dismissed, but reviews, formatting/truncation parity and significance of these exact contrasts remain unresolved. Full LangPTune versus NoProfile-CL instead uses separately trained decoder weights and different training settings. ([v2 Tables 2/4, §§4.2.1, 4.5.1; Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2))

Two other distinctions prevent overstatement. Reducing **global training-set size from 100% to 0.1%** is not a per-user sparsity experiment. The human interpretability test finds **58.89%** binary next-movie choice accuracy for trained profiles versus **57.11%** raw history and **54.67%** zero-shot profiles, with trained-versus-raw **p=0.624** and trained-versus-zero-shot **p=0.201**. Those nonsignificant comparisons and shorter reading times concern a readability/usefulness trade-off, not proof of superior ranking or faithful transaction summaries. ([v2 §4.5.2/Fig.4; §4.6/Tables 5–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.SS6))

## Financial evaluation bounds the meaning of an eventual result

### Investors Are (Not) Always Right separates predicting purchases from earning returns

Sanz-Cruzado, McCreadie, Droukas, Macdonald and Ounis compare transaction-based and customer-independent profitability metrics theoretically and empirically. Theorem 5.6 establishes **zero correlation over all possible valid user–ranking pairs at a fixed time/horizon**, under its assumptions. The authors use “independence,” but zero covariance alone is not general statistical independence; the safe substantive conclusion is **no guaranteed positive relationship**, not a universal law about actual investors. ([TOIS §5.3, Theorem 5.6](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-5-3))

The empirical study uses FAR-Trans and **twelve algorithms**, adding **customer profile similarity (CPS)** to the original eleven-method inventory. The main protocol has **61 temporal variants**, a six-month horizon, binary novel-acquisition relevance and test-activity/pricing filters. Hyperparameters are again selected for six-month ROI at the three dates described above. The article states origins from **1 August 2019 to end-November 2021**, spaced two weeks apart; those statements do not yield an unambiguous literal 61-origin schedule. A complete date list remains a reproduction question. CPS also uses demographic information that the article's Data Statement says could not be publicly shared. ([§6.1–6.3](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6); [Data Statement](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-13))

Unlike the workshop paper, this article supplies explicit metric equations: binary purchase gain with logarithmic rank discount, an equally weighted top-k portfolio, and monthly conversion **`(1 + ROI)^(30 / horizon_days) − 1`**. The reported pooled correlation between **nDCG@10 and monthly ROI@10 is −0.13**, over approximately **1.5 million user × algorithm × temporal-variant values**, with authors reporting **p < 0.05**. This is not a correlation over only twelve model means. Repeated users and overlapping horizons mean that the pooled count should not be treated automatically as independent observations; the literature notes did not recalculate the uncertainty. ([§6.2/Eqs.7–12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6-2); [§7/Fig.4, p.51:23](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

Table 5 repeats shared FAR-Trans baseline values, including **LightGCN 0.3404 nDCG / 0.0004 monthly ROI**, **popularity 0.2710 / 0.0006**, and **random forest 0.0237 / 0.0259**. CPS gives **0.2722 / 0.0026**. These are useful metric contrasts, not a second independent demonstration of representation gains. The article's synthetic effective-investor experiment changes the pooled correlation to **+0.13**; date-specific correlations vary approximately **−0.65 to +0.4**. Thus a universally negative empirical relation is also unsupported. ([§8.1/Table 5](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#tab5); [§9.2/Fig.7](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-9-2); [§10/Fig.8](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-10))

Limitations include one institution, partial portfolios, omitted dividend/coupon income, equal-allocation/customer-independent profitability and simplified common investment horizons. The authors explicitly say abandoning transaction-based evaluation is premature. For this RQ, improved nDCG@10 would mean **better ranking of future observed purchases**, not necessarily higher profits, suitability, risk reduction or welfare. The article contains no LLM-summary experiment or sparse-specific representation result. ([§12 and limitations](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-12))

### Conv-FinRe is an investigated alternative with a different target

**Conv-FinRe: A Conversational and Longitudinal Benchmark for Utility-Grounded Financial Recommendation** is verified as a **SIGIR 2026** publication. Experimental claims here use **arXiv v2**, a pre-camera-ready version. The publisher-deposited record has **thirteen authors**, while the arXiv version has **fourteen**, including **Rosie Guo** rather than the publication's **Yuqing Guo**, and **Xue Liu**, absent from the publication metadata. Their identities/reasons for the differences are not inferred; both full lists appear in [reference_verification.md](reference_verification.md#6-conv-finre--investigated-alternative). ([Publisher-deposited record](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3805712.3808658); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16990))

This benchmark combines real market prices with **ten human participants' simulator decisions**, not FAR-Trans brokerage purchases. Ten stocks and **23 steps per user** yield **230 prefix-conditioned instances**, **270 unique turns** and **3,450 prefix-expanded turns**. Onboarding and later dialogues are generated from profiles and decision trajectories, rather than collected natural human-advisor conversations. Models rerank the fixed stock set using profile/history, market and advisor information. Utility combines standardized seven-day return with individual volatility/drawdown penalties, whose parameters are fitted over each participant's **full longitudinal trajectory**. ([v2 §§3.1–3.3/Tables 2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3))

Metrics include **utility-gain uNDCG over the full candidate set**, choice MRR/HR@1/HR@3 and Kendall τ against advisor rankings. Table 4 reports **Llama-3.3-70B uNDCG 0.97 ± 0.00**, while the finance-specific **XuanYuan3** has **MRR 0.65 ± 0.03** and **HR@1 0.54 ± 0.03**. The inspected caption/text does not clearly identify the ± estimator, so these are retained as reported uncertainty, not relabeled standard errors. History/no-history results are model-dependent: some improve, some barely change, and some lose utility alignment. Removing history changes information; it is not a summary-versus-structured contrast. ([v2 §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS4); [Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.T4); [§4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S4.SS3))

The small repeated-prefix sample, generated dialogue and retrospective utility calibration limit transfer. Full-trajectory fitting raises a point-in-time question if adapted to prospective prediction, without establishing a measured leakage effect in this diagnostic benchmark. The signed-utility equations do not document a nonnegative gain transformation, so conventional binary-nDCG bounds cannot be assumed; **0.97 is not comparable with FAR-Trans's 0.3404**. This paper is retained as adjacent evaluation context and excluded from the core five because Investors supplies more direct FAR-Trans metric evidence, while LangPTune better addresses the representation question. ([v2 §§3.2–3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S3.SS2); [§5](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16990v2#S5))

## The preparation supports a bounded, two-sided research gap

**Among the studies inspected, we did not find a same-information comparison of LLM-generated transaction-history summaries versus structured-history features for a pre-cutoff sparse FAR-Trans cohort, evaluated on future-purchase nDCG@10 under matched users, candidates and downstream ranking conditions.** LangPTune is the closest methodological precedent because it tests bypassing the profile generator, including frozen-decoder variants; FLARKO is closest in dataset/application. Neither establishes the requested financial effect. UPR's lower nDCG than MF, LangPTune's direct-history advantage and FLARKO's mixed context results make a negative or null outcome scientifically informative. No expected effect size can be transferred across their different relevance definitions, cutoffs and candidate sets. ([LangPTune v2 Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4); [FLARKO Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2); [UPR Table 2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.753.pdf))

The remaining preparation task is to clarify the permitted comparison once the class protocol is available: historical information, sparse counting unit, new versus repeat purchases, candidate availability and what “fixed ranker” means. [research_gap.md](research_gap.md) records these as **pending controls**, not an approved experiment or an invented official split.

**Scope:** Task2 literature preparation; bibliography, version and claim audit.

## What “verified” means in these notes

No paper experiment, significance test, code implementation or figure coordinate was independently replicated during synthesis.

### Access-status summary

| Study | Original academic text documented as read | Publication metadata status | Final-text boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| FAR-Trans | arXiv v1 HTML, main text through conclusion; local PDF first-page identity checked | arXiv, official workshop and institutional record | Workshop acceptance verified; separate proceedings DOI not verified; no claim of a separate publisher version |
| FLARKO | arXiv v1 HTML and local v1 PDF, main methods/results/conclusion | ACM-deposited Crossref and arXiv related DOI | ACM landing/PDF blocked (403); final-version equivalence unchecked |

| Conv-FinRe | arXiv v1/v2 HTML; findings use v2 | ACM-deposited Crossref; arXiv acceptance/version record | Final ACM pages/PDF blocked (403); author-list and possible text changes unresolved |

## 1. FAR-Trans — selected foundation

**Complete citation:** Javier Sanz-Cruzado, Nikolaos Droukas, and Richard McCreadie. **2024.** *FAR-Trans: An Investment Dataset for Financial Asset Recommendation.* **IJCAI-24 Workshop on Recommender Systems in Finance (Fin-RecSys)**, Jeju, Republic of Korea, **4 August 2024**. Original evidence version: **arXiv:2407.08692v1**, submitted **11 July 2024**. Cite the workshop, not IJCAI main track. No page range or proceedings DOI was verified in the inspected records. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08692); [official workshop](https://sites.google.com/view/fin-recsys2024/); [program](https://sites.google.com/view/fin-recsys2024/program))

**Identifiers:** **10.48550/arXiv.2407.08692** is the **arXiv/preprint DOI**, not a proceedings DOI. **10.5525/gla.researchdata.1658** is the **dataset DOI**, not the paper DOI. The institutional publication record has a June metadata value, whereas the official workshop date is 4 August; the latter is used for the event. Its `Mccreadie` capitalization is normalized to the article's **McCreadie**, not treated as a different author. ([Publication record](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/id/eprint/328250); [dataset record](https://researchdata.gla.ac.uk/1658/))

**Reading boundary:** `far_trans.md` documents original HTML abstract, introduction, dataset construction, all §5 methods/results including Tables 1–2 and complete §6 conclusion. A second request exposed the conclusion after initial output truncation. `remaining_studies.md` checked the local PDF's first page for identity; it did not claim a second complete PDF reading.

| Claims used | Supporting source locations |
|---|---|
| Data scope; 806 assets, 321 invested assets, 29,090 customers, 388,049 transactions, 228,913 acquisitions, 159,136 sales, 703,303 prices | [§3/Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S3.T1) |

| New-to-user purchase target; binary acquisitions; 61 origins; six-month tests; repeat filtering; eligible users/assets | [§5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS1), [§5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1) |

| Purchase/profitability distinction and future work | [§6](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S6) |

**Unresolved:** Table 1 says 806 assets while §3.2 says 807; local traded counts differ from the paper. The “unique” transaction-count key is not fully defined. Exact origin list, candidate counts, nested tuning chronology and sparse-specific outcomes are absent from the inspected text. Reconstructed events imply a potential point-in-time issue, not a measured leakage magnitude. Separate publisher DOI **not verified** is not proof that none exists.

## 2. FLARKO — selected same-dataset LLM prior work

**Complete publication citation:** Fernando Spadea and Oshani Seneviratne. **2025.** *Aligning Language Models with Investor and Market Behavior for Financial Recommendations.* In **Proceedings of the 6th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '25)**, ACM, **509–517**. Conference: **15–18 November 2025**, Singapore. **Publication DOI: [10.1145/3768292.3770399](https://doi.org/10.1145/3768292.3770399)**. ACM-deposited metadata: online **14 November 2025**, print **15 November 2025**. **FLARKO is the framework name**, not a title prefix. ([Crossref](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3768292.3770399))

**Preprint identity:** same title and two authors, **arXiv:2510.15993v1**, submitted **14 October 2025**; separate **arXiv DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2510.15993**. The local PDF includes an ICAIF bibliographic block and DOI, but it is the **v1 author version used for findings**, not an independently compared final publisher PDF. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15993))

**Reading boundary:** original HTML abstract, §§3–5 method, §§6–7 experiments and complete §8 conclusion; local nine-page PDF main text, Tables 2–4 and results/conclusion. Initial HTML truncation was followed by reading the saved remainder. ACM landing and PDF requests returned 403; Crossref supplies publication metadata, not hidden full-text access.

| Claims used | Supporting source locations |
|---|---|
| PKG transaction fields; MKG metadata/ten-week price aggregates; JSON-LD; 5,000-triple cap; pre-date filtering | [§3.1/Figs.2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S3.SS1), local PDF p.4 |
| Three output ISINs; 180-day purchase-and-positive-return KTO labels | [§3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S3.SS2), [§4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S4), PDF pp.4–5 |
| Train/test dates, conventional baselines, Hits@3 variants | [§6.1–6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS1), PDF p.6 |
