| Centralized PKG/Combined scores; distinct maxima; Nothing Comb@3 0.3718 ± 0.0547 | [§7.1/Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T2), PDF p.7; ± is standard error of a proportion |
| Federated input-specific results | [§7.2/Tables 3–4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S7.T3), PDF p.8; follow table captions where prose cross-references conflict |

## 3. ACL UPR — selected profile-construction precedent

18:

21: **What it answers:** task-specific optimization can improve language-profile pipelines; direct-history and compressed-profile trade-offs can be measured; summaries need not win. **What it does not answer:** the effect of transaction summaries versus tabular/structured features on sparse FAR-Trans purchase nDCG@10. 22: 
23: The decisive counterexample is **v2 Table 4: NoProfile-CL NDCG@20 0.0543 > 512-token LangPTune 0.0494**, Movie-TV/Llama. Under the frozen decoder, NoProfile-0 **0.0372** exceeds zero-shot profile **0.0231**, while generator-trained RLSO gives **0.0377**; unresolved field/truncation parity prevents a fully information-matched interpretation. 29: PKG/MKG/Combined/Nothing ablations change information rather than its encoding. 32: 
33: | Study | What it contributes | What remains unanswered for this RQ |
34: |---|---|---|

36: | ACL UPR | Concrete review-to-profile-to-predictor pipeline; editability and information-loss concerns | Warm-start ratings and condensed test lists; ≥5 training reviews; different model/information baselines. 37: | Investors | Explicit distinction between predicting purchases and price-based return; nDCG/ROI formulas and temporal analysis | No summary arm; shared FAR-Trans baseline results do not independently replicate a summary effect. [§§6–8, 12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6) |
38: | Conv-FinRe | Conversational context and multi-view financial evaluation; model-dependent history effects | Ten-person simulator, generated dialogue, retrospective utility reference and uNDCG; no FAR-Trans or information-matched summary comparison. 39: 
40: ## Task1 motivates sparsity without fixing a future cohort
41: 
42: The local measurements are **full-release descriptive evidence**: 29,090 transaction customers; median **three total events/two Buys**; **21,237 (73.00%)** with 1–3 Buys, **23,663 (81.34%)** with 1–5 and **25,736 (88.47%)** with 1–10. 43:

49:

51: 
52: - [ ] **Fixed users:** freeze the same eligible evaluation users/user–date instances for both arms. Define sparse membership using historical data only. 53: - [ ] **Fixed candidates:** use the same candidate assets per user/date, availability rules, seen-item masking, and any sampling. Resolve invalid/duplicate recommendations consistently. Neither 320 locally traded nor 806 metadata assets automatically defines the historical candidate universe.
54: - [ ] **Fixed item information:** provide the same permitted asset attributes and time-valid snapshots to both representations and candidate encoders. 55: - [ ] **Fixed train/history window:** use identical pre-cutoff events and history duration, with the same timestamp boundary, event types and treatment of repetitions. Separate training, validation and future outcomes chronologically according to the forthcoming class protocol. Filter before fitting preprocessing, computing popularity or generating summaries.
56: - [ ] **Baseline information equivalence:** the structured comparator must be allowed the **same underlying event fields and metadata**, including amounts, units, timing and buy/sell status if the summary sees them. 57: - [ ] **Fixed downstream ranker:** explicitly distinguish **identical frozen fitted weights** from **the same scoring architecture/objective with separate fitting**. 59: - [ ] **Pre-cutoff sparse counting unit:** declare all transaction events, Buy events or distinct bought assets, and whether a finite history window applies. If both buys and sells enter summaries, report total historical events as well as Buy counts. Recompute after the official cutoff/item scope is known; do not select on full-release activity.
60: - [ ] **Matched historical provenance:** treat reconstructed/adjusted events and estimated fields consistently in both arms. Separate an event's assigned date from evidence it was actually known then. Avoid verbalizing inferred holdings or risk traits as directly observed facts.
61: - [ ] **Controlled summary generation:** record model/version, prompt, decoding and length limits; ground summaries in permitted records and assess unsupported additions/omissions. Check external/pretraining knowledge asymmetry. Fluency or shorter reading time alone is not faithfulness or predictive accuracy.
62: - [ ] **Paired and temporally aware assessment:** compare nDCG differences on matched instances; account for recurrent users and overlapping windows when later estimating uncertainty. 65: These controls are **inferences for later preparation**, not procedures already validated for the exact RQ. 66: 
67: ## No official split or expected improvement is inferred
68: 
69: The class cutoff/split, horizon, sparse threshold, candidate policy, repeat-purchase rule and allowed feature sources remain pending. FAR-Trans's **61 temporal variants from 1 August 2019** and FLARKO's **December 2021–2022 test interval** are each source-specific protocols. Investors' additional last-origin statement does not resolve the exact date-list inconsistency. None is promoted to an official class split. 70: 
71: The RQ remains about **purchase prediction, not profit**. ([Investors §§7, 12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))
72: 
73: **Negative and null outcomes would be informative.** A negative result under matched conditions would show that the chosen summary pipeline loses or distorts useful predictive information in that cohort; it would not refute every possible language representation. 74: 
75: **Provenance:** AI-assisted synthesis by OpenCode (`openai/gpt-6-astra`) from the existing evidence notes and Task1 outputs. The user personally verified transaction7590224 and asset metadata; personal paper verification is pending. No numerical effect for the proposed FAR-Trans comparison has been measured in this preparation.

([LangPTune v2 §§4.2, 4.5/Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2); [FLARKO §§3–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1); [FAR-Trans §5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2); [Investors §6](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6))

## No official split or expected improvement is inferred

The class cutoff/split, horizon, sparse threshold, candidate policy, repeat-purchase rule and allowed feature sources remain pending. FAR-Trans's **61 temporal variants from 1 August 2019** and FLARKO's **December 2021–2022 test interval** are each source-specific protocols. Investors' additional last-origin statement does not resolve the exact date-list inconsistency. None is promoted to an official class split. Published aggregate LightGCN **0.3404** is not an expected sparse-cohort replication score. ([FAR-Trans §5.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08692v1#S5.SS2.SSS1); [FLARKO §6.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.15993v1#S6.SS1); [Investors §6.1](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-6-1); [Task1 protocol status](dataset_inventory.md#sources-read-and-scope))

The RQ remains about **purchase prediction, not profit**. A positive nDCG@10 difference would support better ranking of subsequently bought assets under the declared protocol; it would not establish better investment returns, risk suitability, causal adoption, interpretability or welfare. Investors reports pooled nDCG/monthly-ROI correlation **−0.13** and cautions against treating one metric family as a proxy for the other, while explicitly retaining transaction evaluation as useful. ([Investors §§7, 12](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3780097#sec-7))

**Negative and null outcomes would be informative.** A negative result under matched conditions would show that the chosen summary pipeline loses or distorts useful predictive information in that cohort; it would not refute every possible language representation. A null estimate with wide uncertainty would be inconclusive, whereas a sufficiently precise near-zero estimate would constrain plausible benefit for the tested setting. A positive result would still require the control checks above before attributing it to representation. LangPTune's compression result makes this a substantive empirical question, not an exercise with a predetermined favorable answer. ([v2 §4.5.1/Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18870v2#S4.T4))

**Provenance:** AI-assisted synthesis by OpenCode (`openai/gpt-6-astra`) from the existing evidence notes and Task1 outputs. The user personally verified transaction7590224 and asset metadata; personal paper verification is pending. No numerical effect for the proposed FAR-Trans comparison has been measured in this preparation.

1786: 12     Conclusion and Recommendations
1787: Enabling a sound and interpretable evaluation is a critical component of FAR systems. However,
1788: multiple competing evaluation methods are currently used by FAR researchers and developers,
1789: with little guidance regarding when and where each approach should be used. This article aims to
1790: bridge that gap by analysing the relations between the two most common evaluation perspectives:
1791: transaction-based and profitability-based evaluation. We showed that these two strategies cannot
1792: be considered equivalent to each other: First, we provided a theoretical proof that these two
1793: evaluation approaches are independent from each other. Then, when we compared these two
1794: perspectives in a realistic experimental setup over a large financial asset pricing and transaction
1795: dataset, we demonstrated a negative correlation between the profitability and transaction-based
1796: metrics across a diverse array of 12 deployed FAR approaches. This highlights that we cannot assume
1797: that customers invest effectively, and therefore, predicting future investment transactions does not
1798: permit customers to increase their wealth—the negative correlation shows that the opposite might
1799: actually happen.
1800:    Through analysis of these models and customer investment behaviour over time, we showed
1801: that customer investment transactions are a problematic data source for evaluation on their own:
1802: there are periods when customers are unable to improve the performance of the market with their
1803: investments and identifying their future investments in those cases might then lead to a decrease
1804: in wealth; Moreover, models are unaware of the customer investment strategy—which can lead to
1805: great variations in returns.
1806:    While it would be premature to suggest that transaction-based evaluation should be abandoned for
1807: FAR systems, our results demonstrate that transaction-based metrics have important limitations that
1808: need to be understood if they are to be useful. Hence, we provide the following recommendations
1809: for researchers and practitioners:
1810: 
1811: ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
1812:  Investors Are (Not) Always Right                                                                             51:39
1813: 
1814:    — Complement Transaction-based Evaluation: Due to the limitations of transaction-based metrics,
1815:      these metrics should not be used alone to evaluate FAR models. At least, researchers and
1816:      practitioners should also evaluate the profitability of their proposed approaches.
1817:    — Consider Changing Market Conditions: Financial markets are in a state of continuous change,
1818:      something that might be even more noticeable with the emergence of global events like
1819:      pandemics or wars (which have a huge impact over the market). Major events influence
1820:      the expectations people have on market segments, prompting customers to change their
1821:      investment positions. Models trained using transaction-based metrics will perform poorly
1822:      during such times, as past and current investment behaviour are no longer similar. In addition,
1823:      sudden market changes might confound profitability prediction algorithms and affect their
1824:      performance. Hence, it is important to report performance over time to reveal when these
1825:      changes occur, and solution developers might wish to consider fall-back strategies during
1826:      such times.
1827:    — Investment Horizons are a Confounding Variable: Different customers plan for different in-
1828:      vestment time horizons (how long they want to hold an asset for). Analysis of our dataset
1829:      indicated that these time horizons are markedly longer than we anticipated, with the peak
1830:      between 15 and 18 months, but with a wide range of horizons being observed. This has sev-
1831:      eral important consequences for evaluation. First, individual customer transactions become
1832:      difficult to interpret, as we cannot know in advance the customer’s envisaged investment
1833:      horizon. Second, aggregate metrics like nDCG conflate customers with different horizons,
1834:      hence models trained based on such metrics will likely perform poorly in practice (since we
1835:      do not know how long to hold a recommended asset for).
1836:    — Know Your Customers: Identifying the strengths and weaknesses of customers as investors is
1837:      fundamental for the identification and development of effective financial asset recommenda-
1838:      tion algorithms. For instance, if customers commonly perform under the market, exploiting
1839:      their past transactions as input of collaborative filtering algorithms might further increase the
1840:      gap between user and market performance. A thorough analysis of the skills and expertise of
1841:      the users is needed to find profitable algorithms.
1842:     As future work, we envisage the creation of an adequate and robust framework for FAR evaluation,
1843: which puts the focus on the customers and their trading strategies. To develop such a framework,
1844: it is necessary to understand what role customer features—such as the effects patterns of spending,
1845: relationship with the financial institutions, risk aversion, trading platform or sector interest—might
1846: have on FAR evaluation. Another line of research might address how the past actions of financial
1847: institutions might affect the evaluation, as past actions of financial advisors might introduce some
1848: biases on the collected datasets (similarly to how the actions of past recommendation policies
1849: introduce selection biases on offline datasets for general domain recommendation [53]).
1850: 
1851: Limitations
1852: We discuss here the limitations of the theoretical and empirical analysis carried in this work. We
1853: focus this discussion on three aspects: the fixed investment horizon, the CI property of transaction-
1854: based metrics and the limitations of the dataset.
1855: Investment Horizon. In our theoretical formulations and experiments, we commonly consider a fixed
1856: investment horizon shared by all customers. As seen in Figure 10, this is a simplification, as people
1857: might consider different holding times for their investments. We have applied this simplification as
1858: it is common practice in the evaluation of financial asset recommendations [3, 31, 44, 71].
1859:     In our experiments, we consider only short-to-mid-term investment horizons, ranging from
1860: 1 month to a year. While Figure 10 suggests that customers in our data hold their investment for
1861: 
1862:                 ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
1863:  51:40                                                                                        J. Sanz-Cruzado et al.
1864: 
1865: even longer times (79.86% of the customers hold their investments for more than 1 year), the time
1866: span of our dataset does not allow us to test longer horizons: for a fixed investment horizon, Δ𝑡,
1867: we would need sufficient data after the last split date of our dataset. For instance, for Δ𝑡 = 2 years,
1868: we would need at least 2 years of data after the last split date of our dataset, November 2021, but
1869: our dataset only has data until November 2022. Therefore, the maximum value of Δ𝑡 we can test
1870: with this dataset is 1 year. Furthermore, it is not possible to move the splits to earlier dates, since
1871: we also need a sufficiently long training period to train the different models: for instance, for the
1872: profitability-based models, we need, at least, Δ𝑡 + 6 months of training data before the first split
1873: date. In our experimental setup, we have 18 months of data before the first split, corresponding to
1874: the minimum period needed for Δ𝑡 = 1 year.
1875:    While customers might take more time to sell their assets, we argue that these shorter horizons
1876: still represent a realistic scenario: while investors might hold their investment for longer, financial
1877: institutions recommend investors to check and rebalance their investment horizons at least once a
1878: year [69]. This periodical check aligns with our investment horizons choices. In addition to this,
1879: the experiments in Section 11 seem to indicate that our findings should generalise when looking at
1880: longer investment horizons.
1881: CI. The profitability-based metrics that we have defined in this work follow the CI property. This
1882: property indicates that the profitability of a recommendation does only depend on the recommended
1883: assets, and not in the customer. We have considered this property as it represents a common
1884: simplification applied in past financial asset recommendation research. However, this simplification
1885: might not always hold in realistic investment scenarios for two reasons:
1886:   (1) Portfolio weights: By considering profitability-based metrics independent of the customer, we
1887:       are assuming that a customer invests the same amount of money on every asset. However,
1888:       this is rarely true in practice. Customers build their investment portfolios by allocating
1889:       different amounts of money according to factors like their risk awareness (for example, a
1890:       very risk-averse investor should allocate more money to safer assets like government bonds
1891:       than to stocks).
1892:   (2) Customer goals: Different customers might also react differently to the same level of prof-
1893:       itability, depending on factors like their initial investment or their goals. For instance, it is
1894:       easier to achieve enough money to buy a videogame console with low returns than it is to
1895:       buy a house.
1896: Any metric considering these two factors would fall into the hybrid metric category—and, are,
1897: therefore, out of the scope of this work. Hybrid metrics capable of considering aspects like portfolio
1898: weights or customer goals require additional customer information that is not easily accessible: for
1899: instance, if we wanted to consider portfolio weights, we would need to estimate how much money
1900: a customer might invest on each asset—even on assets on which the customer has never invested
1901: before. We envision exploring these hybrid metrics as future work.
1902:    Another alternative to evaluate customers according to their goals/portfolio allocation might
1903: rely on expert ratings to evaluate the models. However, this evaluation is unfeasible on a large
1904: dataset like the one explored in this work: we would need expert scores for 29,090 customers at 61
1905: points in time for 12 algorithms. The cost would be even bigger if we consider the experiment with
1906: synthetic users and the different time horizons.
1907: Dataset Limitations. Our analysis is limited to a single investment dataset, FAR-Trans [50]. As far as
1908: we are aware, FAR-Trans is currently the only public large-scale investment dataset containing both
1909: asset information and customer investment transactions. This dataset has limitations. First, it only
1910: provides a partial view of the investors’ portfolios, representing investments in publicly-traded
1911: 
1912: ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
1913:  Investors Are (Not) Always Right                                                                                     51:41
1914: 
1915: financial assets that might pose a risk to the investor. Banking institutions commonly have privately
1916: created risk-less assets that can complement the riskier stocks or funds and are not available in the
1917: data. And second, it does only provide pricing information about the assets, ignoring other factors
1918: that might influence their profitability, such as stock dividend or bond coupon payments.
1919:    However, it still represents a real-world dataset, representing the day-to-day operation of invest-
1920: ments in a large financial institution. While the global correlations between transaction-based and
1921: profitability-based metrics might change if we analyse the same data for a different institution, we
1922: expect our main conclusion to remain the same: investment transactions represent a problematic
1923: source of data for evaluating financial asset recommendations, as they do not reflect whether
1924: customers earn money with them.
1925:

1927: The dataset used for supporting the experiments in this article is available at https://doi.org/10.

12     Conclusion and Recommendations
Enabling a sound and interpretable evaluation is a critical component of FAR systems. However,
multiple competing evaluation methods are currently used by FAR researchers and developers,
with little guidance regarding when and where each approach should be used. This article aims to
bridge that gap by analysing the relations between the two most common evaluation perspectives:
transaction-based and profitability-based evaluation. We showed that these two strategies cannot
be considered equivalent to each other: First, we provided a theoretical proof that these two
evaluation approaches are independent from each other. Then, when we compared these two
perspectives in a realistic experimental setup over a large financial asset pricing and transaction
dataset, we demonstrated a negative correlation between the profitability and transaction-based
metrics across a diverse array of 12 deployed FAR approaches. This highlights that we cannot assume
that customers invest effectively, and therefore, predicting future investment transactions does not
permit customers to increase their wealth—the negative correlation shows that the opposite might
actually happen.
   Through analysis of these models and customer investment behaviour over time, we showed
that customer investment transactions are a problematic data source for evaluation on their own:
there are periods when customers are unable to improve the performance of the market with their
investments and identifying their future investments in those cases might then lead to a decrease
in wealth; Moreover, models are unaware of the customer investment strategy—which can lead to
great variations in returns.

12     Conclusion and Recommendations
Enabling a sound and interpretable evaluation is a critical component of FAR systems. However,
multiple competing evaluation methods are currently used by FAR researchers and developers,
with little guidance regarding when and where each approach should be used. This article aims to
bridge that gap by analysing the relations between the two most common evaluation perspectives:
transaction-based and profitability-based evaluation. We showed that these two strategies cannot
be considered equivalent to each other: First, we provided a theoretical proof that these two
evaluation approaches are independent from each other. Then, when we compared these two
perspectives in a realistic experimental setup over a large financial asset pricing and transaction
dataset, we demonstrated a negative correlation between the profitability and transaction-based
metrics across a diverse array of 12 deployed FAR approaches. This highlights that we cannot assume
that customers invest effectively, and therefore, predicting future investment transactions does not
permit customers to increase their wealth—the negative correlation shows that the opposite might
actually happen.
   Through analysis of these models and customer investment behaviour over time, we showed
that customer investment transactions are a problematic data source for evaluation on their own:
there are periods when customers are unable to improve the performance of the market with their
investments and identifying their future investments in those cases might then lead to a decrease
in wealth; Moreover, models are unaware of the customer investment strategy—which can lead to
great variations in returns.
   While it would be premature to suggest that transaction-based evaluation should be abandoned for
FAR systems, our results demonstrate that transaction-based metrics have important limitations that
need to be understood if they are to be useful. Hence, we provide the following recommendations
for researchers and practitioners:

ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
 Investors Are (Not) Always Right                                                                             51:39

   — Complement Transaction-based Evaluation: Due to the limitations of transaction-based metrics,
     these metrics should not be used alone to evaluate FAR models. At least, researchers and
     practitioners should also evaluate the profitability of their proposed approaches.
   — Consider Changing Market Conditions: Financial markets are in a state of continuous change,
     something that might be even more noticeable with the emergence of global events like
     pandemics or wars (which have a huge impact over the market). Major events influence
     the expectations people have on market segments, prompting customers to change their
     investment positions. Models trained using transaction-based metrics will perform poorly
     during such times, as past and current investment behaviour are no longer similar. In addition,
     sudden market changes might confound profitability prediction algorithms and affect their
     performance. Hence, it is important to report performance over time to reveal when these
     changes occur, and solution developers might wish to consider fall-back strategies during
     such times.
   — Investment Horizons are a Confounding Variable: Different customers plan for different in-
     vestment time horizons (how long they want to hold an asset for). Analysis of our dataset
     indicated that these time horizons are markedly longer than we anticipated, with the peak
     between 15 and 18 months, but with a wide range of horizons being observed. This has sev-
     eral important consequences for evaluation. First, individual customer transactions become
     difficult to interpret, as we cannot know in advance the customer’s envisaged investment
     horizon. Second, aggregate metrics like nDCG conflate customers with different horizons,
     hence models trained based on such metrics will likely perform poorly in practice (since we
     do not know how long to hold a recommended asset for).
   — Know Your Customers: Identifying the strengths and weaknesses of customers as investors is
     fundamental for the identification and development of effective financial asset recommenda-
     tion algorithms. For instance, if customers commonly perform under the market, exploiting
     their past transactions as input of collaborative filtering algorithms might further increase the
     gap between user and market performance. A thorough analysis of the skills and expertise of
     the users is needed to find profitable algorithms.
    As future work, we envisage the creation of an adequate and robust framework for FAR evaluation,
which puts the focus on the customers and their trading strategies. To develop such a framework,
it is necessary to understand what role customer features—such as the effects patterns of spending,
relationship with the financial institutions, risk aversion, trading platform or sector interest—might
have on FAR evaluation. Another line of research might address how the past actions of financial
institutions might affect the evaluation, as past actions of financial advisors might introduce some
biases on the collected datasets (similarly to how the actions of past recommendation policies
introduce selection biases on offline datasets for general domain recommendation [53]).

Limitations
We discuss here the limitations of the theoretical and empirical analysis carried in this work. We
focus this discussion on three aspects: the fixed investment horizon, the CI property of transaction-
based metrics and the limitations of the dataset.
Investment Horizon. In our theoretical formulations and experiments, we commonly consider a fixed
investment horizon shared by all customers. As seen in Figure 10, this is a simplification, as people
might consider different holding times for their investments. We have applied this simplification as
it is common practice in the evaluation of financial asset recommendations [3, 31, 44, 71].
    In our experiments, we consider only short-to-mid-term investment horizons, ranging from
1 month to a year. While Figure 10 suggests that customers in our data hold their investment for

                ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
 51:40                                                                                        J. Sanz-Cruzado et al.

even longer times (79.86% of the customers hold their investments for more than 1 year), the time
span of our dataset does not allow us to test longer horizons: for a fixed investment horizon, Δ𝑡,
we would need sufficient data after the last split date of our dataset. For instance, for Δ𝑡 = 2 years,
we would need at least 2 years of data after the last split date of our dataset, November 2021, but
our dataset only has data until November 2022. Therefore, the maximum value of Δ𝑡 we can test
with this dataset is 1 year. Furthermore, it is not possible to move the splits to earlier dates, since
we also need a sufficiently long training period to train the different models: for instance, for the
profitability-based models, we need, at least, Δ𝑡 + 6 months of training data before the first split
date. In our experimental setup, we have 18 months of data before the first split, corresponding to
the minimum period needed for Δ𝑡 = 1 year.
   While customers might take more time to sell their assets, we argue that these shorter horizons
still represent a realistic scenario: while investors might hold their investment for longer, financial
institutions recommend investors to check and rebalance their investment horizons at least once a
year [69]. This periodical check aligns with our investment horizons choices. In addition to this,
the experiments in Section 11 seem to indicate that our findings should generalise when looking at
longer investment horizons.
CI. The profitability-based metrics that we have defined in this work follow the CI property. This
property indicates that the profitability of a recommendation does only depend on the recommended
assets, and not in the customer. We have considered this property as it represents a common
simplification applied in past financial asset recommendation research. However, this simplification
might not always hold in realistic investment scenarios for two reasons:
  (1) Portfolio weights: By considering profitability-based metrics independent of the customer, we
      are assuming that a customer invests the same amount of money on every asset. However,
      this is rarely true in practice. Customers build their investment portfolios by allocating
      different amounts of money according to factors like their risk awareness (for example, a
      very risk-averse investor should allocate more money to safer assets like government bonds
      than to stocks).
  (2) Customer goals: Different customers might also react differently to the same level of prof-
      itability, depending on factors like their initial investment or their goals. For instance, it is
      easier to achieve enough money to buy a videogame console with low returns than it is to
      buy a house.
Any metric considering these two factors would fall into the hybrid metric category—and, are,
therefore, out of the scope of this work. Hybrid metrics capable of considering aspects like portfolio
weights or customer goals require additional customer information that is not easily accessible: for
instance, if we wanted to consider portfolio weights, we would need to estimate how much money
a customer might invest on each asset—even on assets on which the customer has never invested
before. We envision exploring these hybrid metrics as future work.
   Another alternative to evaluate customers according to their goals/portfolio allocation might
rely on expert ratings to evaluate the models. However, this evaluation is unfeasible on a large
dataset like the one explored in this work: we would need expert scores for 29,090 customers at 61
points in time for 12 algorithms. The cost would be even bigger if we consider the experiment with
synthetic users and the different time horizons.
Dataset Limitations. Our analysis is limited to a single investment dataset, FAR-Trans [50]. As far as
we are aware, FAR-Trans is currently the only public large-scale investment dataset containing both
asset information and customer investment transactions. This dataset has limitations. First, it only
provides a partial view of the investors’ portfolios, representing investments in publicly-traded

ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 2, Article 51. Publication date: January 2026.
 Investors Are (Not) Always Right                                                                                     51:41

financial assets that might pose a risk to the investor. Banking institutions commonly have privately
created risk-less assets that can complement the riskier stocks or funds and are not available in the
data. And second, it does only provide pricing information about the assets, ignoring other factors
that might influence their profitability, such as stock dividend or bond coupon payments.
   However, it still represents a real-world dataset, representing the day-to-day operation of invest-
ments in a large financial institution. While the global correlations between transaction-based and
profitability-based metrics might change if we analyse the same data for a different institution, we
expect our main conclusion to remain the same: investment transactions represent a problematic
source of data for evaluating financial asset recommendations, as they do not reflect whether
customers earn money with them.

Data Statement
The dataset used for supporting the experiments in this article is available at https://doi.org/10.
5525/gla.researchdata.1658. The demographic information about the users could not be shared due
to its sensitive nature.

**Expertise in agent capabilities**, enabling precise integration with external tools in both thinking and unthinking modes and achieving leading performance among open-source models in complex agent-based tasks. - **Support of 100+ languages and dialects** with strong capabilities for **multilingual instruction following** and **translation**. ## Model Overview **Qwen3-1.7B** has the following features: - Type: Causal Language Models - Context Length: 32,768 For more details, including benchmark evaluation, hardware requirements, and inference performance, please refer to our [blog](https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen3/), [GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3), and [Documentation](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). > [!TIP] > If you encounter significant endless repetitions, please refer to the [Best Practices](#best-practices) section for optimal sampling parameters, and set the ``presence_penalty`` to 1.5. ## Quickstart The code of Qwen3 has been in the latest Hugging Face `transformers` and we advise you to use the latest version of `transformers`. With `transformers<4.51.0`, you will encounter the following error: ``` KeyError: 'qwen3' ``` The following contains a code snippet illustrating how to use the model generate content based on given inputs. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B" # load the tokenizer and the model tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_name, torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto" ) # prepare the model input prompt = "Give me a short introduction to large language model." messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": prompt} ] text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=True # Switches between thinking and non-thinking modes. Default is True. ) model_inputs = tokenizer([text], return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) # conduct text completion generated_ids = model.generate( **model_inputs, max_new_tokens=32768 ) output_ids = generated_ids[0][len(model_inputs.input_ids[0]):].tolist() # parsing thinking content try: # rindex finding 151668 () index = len(output_ids) - output_ids[::-1].index(151668) except ValueError: index = 0 thinking_content = tokenizer.decode(output_ids[:index], skip_special_tokens=True).strip("\n") content = tokenizer.decode(output_ids[index:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip("\n") print("thinking content:", thinking_content) print("content:", content) ``` For deployment, you can use `sglang>=0.4.6.post1` or `vllm>=0.8.5` or to create an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint: - SGLang: ```shell python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --reasoning-parser qwen3 ``` - vLLM: ```shell vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --enable-reasoning --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1 ``` For local use, applications such as Ollama, LMStudio, MLX-LM, llama.cpp, and KTransformers have also supported Qwen3. ## Switching Between Thinking and Non-Thinking Mode > [!TIP] > The `enable_thinking` switch is also available in APIs created by SGLang and vLLM. > Please refer to our documentation for [SGLang](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/deployment/sglang.html#thinking-non-thinking-modes) and [vLLM](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/deployment/vllm.html#thinking-non-thinking-modes) users. ### `enable_thinking=True` By default, Qwen3 has thinking capabilities enabled, similar to QwQ-32B. This means the model will use its reasoning abilities to enhance the quality of generated responses. For example, when explicitly setting `enable_thinking=True` or leaving it as the default value in `tokenizer.apply_chat_template`, the model will engage its thinking mode. ```python text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=True # True is the default value for enable_thinking ) ``` In this mode, the model will generate think content wrapped in a `...` block, followed by the final response. > [!NOTE] > For thinking mode, use `Temperature=0.6`, `TopP=0.95`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0` (the default setting in `generation_config.json`). **DO NOT use greedy decoding**, as it can lead to performance degradation and endless repetitions. For more detailed guidance, please refer to the [Best Practices](#best-practices) section. ### `enable_thinking=False` We provide a hard switch to strictly disable the model's thinking behavior, aligning its functionality with the previous Qwen2.5-Instruct models. This mode is particularly useful in scenarios where disabling thinking is essential for enhancing efficiency. ```python text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False # Setting enable_thinking=False disables thinking mode ) ``` In this mode, the model will not generate any think content and will not include a `...` block. > [!NOTE] > For non-thinking mode, we suggest using `Temperature=0.7`, `TopP=0.8`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0`. For more detailed guidance, please refer to the [Best Practices](#best-practices) section. ### Advanced Usage: Switching Between Thinking and Non-Thinking Modes via User Input We provide a soft switch mechanism that allows users to dynamically control the model's behavior when `enable_thinking=True`. Specifically, you can add `/think` and `/no_think` to user prompts or system messages to switch the model's thinking mode from turn to turn. The model will follow the most recent instruction in multi-turn conversations. Here is an example of a multi-turn conversation: ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer class QwenChatbot: def __init__(self, model_name="Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B"): self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name) self.history = [] def generate_response(self, user_input): messages = self.history + [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}] text = self.tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True ) inputs = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt") response_ids = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32768)[0][len(inputs.input_ids[0]):].tolist() response = self.tokenizer.decode(response_ids, skip_special_tokens=True) # Update history self.history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input}) self.history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response}) return response # Example Usage if __name__ == "__main__": chatbot = QwenChatbot() # First input (without /think or /no_think tags, thinking mode is enabled by default) user_input_1 = "How many r's in strawberries?" print(f"User: {user_input_1}") response_1 = chatbot.generate_response(user_input_1) print(f"Bot: {response_1}") print("----------------------") # Second input with /no_think user_input_2 = "Then, how many r's in blueberries? /no_think" print(f"User: {user_input_2}") response_2 = chatbot.generate_response(user_input_2) print(f"Bot: {response_2}") print("----------------------") # Third input with /think user_input_3 = "Really? /think" print(f"User: {user_input_3}") response_3 = chatbot.generate_response(user_input_3) print(f"Bot: {response_3}") ``` > [!NOTE] > For API compatibility, when `enable_thinking=True`, regardless of whether the user uses `/think` or `/no_think`, the model will always output a block wrapped in `...`. However, the content inside this block may be empty if thinking is disabled. > When `enable_thinking=False`, the soft switches are not valid. Regardless of any `/think` or `/no_think` tags input by the user, the model will not generate think content and will not include a `...` block. ## Agentic Use Qwen3 excels in tool calling capabilities. We recommend using [Qwen-Agent](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Agent) to make the best use of agentic ability of Qwen3. Qwen-Agent encapsulates tool-calling templates and tool-calling parsers internally, greatly reducing coding complexity. To define the available tools, you can use the MCP configuration file, use the integrated tool of Qwen-Agent, or integrate other tools by yourself. ```python from qwen_agent.agents import Assistant # Define LLM llm_cfg = { 'model': 'Qwen3-1.7B', # Use the endpoint provided by Alibaba Model Studio: # 'model_type': 'qwen_dashscope', # 'api_key': os.getenv('DASHSCOPE_API_KEY'), # Use a custom endpoint compatible with OpenAI API: 'model_server': 'http://localhost:8000/v1', # api_base 'api_key': 'EMPTY', # Other parameters: # 'generate_cfg': { # # Add: When the response content is `this is the thoughtthis is the answer; # # Do not add: When the response has been separated by reasoning_content and content. # 'thought_in_content': True, # }, } # Define Tools tools = [ {'mcpServers': { # You can specify the MCP configuration file 'time': { 'command': 'uvx', 'args': ['mcp-server-time', '--local-timezone=Asia/Shanghai'] }, "fetch": { "command": "uvx", "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"] } } }, 'code_interpreter', # Built-in tools ] # Define Agent bot = Assistant(llm=llm_cfg, function_list=tools) # Streaming generation messages = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/ Introduce the latest developments of Qwen'}] for responses in bot.run(messages=messages): pass print(responses) ``` ## Best Practices To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings: 1. **Sampling Parameters**: - For thinking mode (`enable_thinking=True`), use `Temperature=0.6`, `TopP=0.95`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0`. **DO NOT use greedy decoding**, as it can lead to performance degradation and endless repetitions. - For non-thinking mode (`enable_thinking=False`), we suggest using `Temperature=0.7`, `TopP=0.8`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0`. - For supported frameworks, you can adjust the `presence_penalty` parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetitions. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance. 2. **Adequate Output Length**: We recommend using an output length of 32,768 tokens for most queries. For benchmarking on highly complex problems, such as those found in math and programming competitions, we suggest setting the max output length to 38,912 tokens. This provides the model with sufficient space to generate detailed and comprehensive responses, thereby enhancing its overall performance. 3. **Standardize Output Format**: We recommend using prompts to standardize model outputs when benchmarking. - **Math Problems**: Include "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}." in the prompt. - **Multiple-Choice Questions**: Add the following JSON structure to the prompt to standardize responses: "Please show your choice in the `answer` field with only the choice letter, e.g., `"answer": "C"`." 4. **No Thinking Content in History**: In multi-turn conversations, the historical model output should only include the final output part and does not need to include the thinking content. It is implemented in the provided chat template in Jinja2. However, for frameworks that do not directly use the Jinja2 chat template, it is up to the developers to ensure that the best practice is followed. ### Citation If you find our work helpful, feel free to give us a cite. ``` @misc{qwen3technicalreport, title={Qwen3 Technical Report}, author={Qwen Team}, year={2025}, eprint={2505.09388}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.CL}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388}, } ```

Great Britain and Northern Ireland

The use of recommender systems to assist in the provision of financial asset and portfolio recommenda-
tions to investors is increasing, spanning a wide range of algorithms and techniques. Several strategies
have been devised for the evaluation of financial asset recommendations, with the two most prominent
perspectives measuring, respectively, (a) the money customers could obtain if they followed the recommen-
dations (profitability-based evaluation) and (b) the ability of models to predict future customer investments
(transaction-based evaluation). If customers are effective investors, we would expect these two perspectives to
be positively correlated. In this article, we explore the actual relationship between these two families of metrics.
Theoretically, we prove that these perspectives are independent. Furthermore, we perform experiments over a
large-scale financial recommendation dataset with real customer investment transactions. Surprisingly, we
find that transaction and profitability-based metrics are, in fact, negatively correlated. Moreover, algorithms
that actively learn from past customer transactions might lose money in the mid-term. A thorough analysis of
model performance and customer transaction patterns over time shows that this is due to customers failing
to consistently beat the market with their investments, with time appearing as an important confounding
variable—since the point of time where recommendations are provided and the investment horizon largely
affect the customer’s investment performance.

+**RQ1:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?
+
+## Research Importance
+
+### Concise paragraph for Section 1
+
+Sparse-history financial recommendation is a useful test of whether language-based representations preserve or improve limited behavioral evidence. FAR-Trans documents a long-tailed activity distribution, with over half its customers making at most three transactions across the observation period [1, §3.3, Fig. 2]. Its benchmark establishes purchase-ranking baselines, while FLARKO demonstrates LLM-based recommendation on FAR-Trans using structured knowledge graphs and purchase/profitability hit metrics [1, §5; 2, §§3–7]. Natural-language profiles can support inspectable recommendations [3], but their compression can reduce ranking accuracy: LangPTune's v2 direct-history comparator exceeds its summarized-profile pipeline in one Movie-TV comparison [4, Table 4]. Among these five studies, we did not find the proposed information-matched comparison for pre-cutoff sparse FAR-Trans users. Testing structured features against summaries, with a deterministic-text control and shared evaluation conditions, would clarify whether the chosen summary pipeline helps purchase ranking or discards useful evidence. Either outcome would bound the usefulness of language-based history representations in this financial setting, without implying a literature-wide novelty claim.
+
+### Evidence and scope behind the argument
+
+- **Meaningful population:** Task 1 measured a full-release median of **2 Buy events**, P75 **4**, and **23,663/29,090 customers (81.34%)** with 1–5 Buys. These local counts motivate a *provisional* low-activity band; they do not establish pre-cutoff eligibility. They differ in counting unit from the paper's total-transaction statistic. See [sparse_user_analysis.md](sparse_user_analysis.md).
+- **Established knowledge:** [1] provides a common financial dataset and eleven non-LLM algorithms; [2] studies graph-grounded LLM recommendations; [3] studies review-based natural-language profiles and profile editing; [4] studies profile-generator/ranker optimization and the information bottleneck; [5] distinguishes transaction relevance from profitability. None of these contributions should be relabelled a controlled sparse-FAR-Trans summary result.
+- **Nearest prior work:** LangPTune is nearest methodologically; FLARKO is nearest in dataset/application. LangPTune's accessible v2 Table 4 reports **NoProfile-CL NDCG@20 0.0543**, versus **0.0494** for the 512-token profile. These are Amazon Movie-TV results, with no significance claim for this exact pair; the direct input is item-metadata text, not the proposed financial structured vector. The final CIKM tables have not been independently checked.
+- **Scientific contrast:** A-versus-C compares two practical representation pipelines using the same permissible source facts. B-versus-C narrows the comparison by retaining the same frozen text encoder and adapter architecture while removing LLM generation. It helps distinguish text encoding/formatting from generated abstraction, but does not prove an internal reasoning mechanism. Encoder differences and unequal retained information after compression remain part of the treatment.
+- **Knowledge contribution:** estimate a paired ranking effect and its uncertainty for a declared population, source-information budget and historical protocol; document when compression, pretrained semantics or unsupported statements might explain the result. This is a scoped empirical contribution, not a promised improvement or general superiority of LLMs.
+
+## Business Value
+
+### Concise paragraph for Section 1
+
+A financial recommendation product owner must decide whether adding an offline LLM-summary stage is worth its cost compared with maintaining structured customer-history features. A few purchases provide limited evidence for personalization, and FAR-Trans's strong popularity baseline cautions against assuming that a more complex representation adds value [1, §5]. Profile research suggests that language may organize behavior into a readable representation, but also documents information loss, hallucinations and latency [3, §§5–8; 4, §4.5]. Here, the proposed benefit is better ranking of future purchases from the same historical facts, not discovery of a customer's true goals or risk tolerance. A reliable improvement at acceptable measured cost would support further offline validation and a supervised product pilot; an adverse or sufficiently precise near-zero result would support retaining the simpler pipeline and avoiding generation and monitoring overhead. Because purchases are behavioral labels, improved nDCG@10 would not establish profitability, suitability, revenue or causal customer benefit [5, §12].
+
+### Practical decision and costs to record
+
+The stakeholder is the **product owner of an asset-discovery/recommendation service**, working with its engineering and model-review teams. This is a research decision about a ranking component, not personal financial advice or a live trading system. Possible benefits of readable histories are hypotheses transferred from review-domain studies, not demonstrated FAR-Trans outcomes. In the proposed experiment, summaries are internal model inputs; human-facing usefulness is not evaluated.
+
+The additional work includes summary generation whenever history changes, text embedding, caching/version invalidation, factuality checks, monitoring and failure handling. Measure generation and embedding time, cache-hit and cold-path latency, storage, token volumes and billed compute alongside ranking time. Caching may move generation outside the request path; it does not eliminate refresh latency, stale summaries or generation cost. Operational risks include invented preferences, lost quantities/recency, identity exposure, and changed output after model revisions. The provisional **US$50 and 48 GPU-hour ceilings** are study planning limits, not an estimate of product ROI, an approved spend or measured expenditure. See [evaluation_plan.md](evaluation_plan.md).
+
+## Positive-result implications
+
+**Research — brief Section 5 paragraph.** If C exceeds A with a positive paired uncertainty interval on the preregistered sparse cohort, the finding would support this specific summary-plus-encoder pipeline under the tested information and scoring conditions. A C-over-B advantage would provide additional evidence for generated abstraction beyond deterministic text encoding; a C-over-A gain without a C-over-B gain would leave that attribution unsupported. Neither pattern establishes universal LLM superiority, an effect in every market regime, or an improvement caused solely by summarization independent of encoder choices [2–4].
+
+**Business — brief Section 5 paragraph.** A reproducible gain would justify further validation only if measured generation/refresh cost, latency, failure rates and factuality are acceptable to the product owner. It would support considering a controlled, supervised pilot rather than automatic deployment. Financial suitability and causal product outcomes would require separate evidence; nDCG@10 alone cannot justify claims of greater returns or revenue [5].
+
+## Negative-result implications
+
+**Research — brief Section 5 paragraph.** A negative C-minus-A effect would show that the tested summary pipeline is less effective than the structured comparator in this setting; loss of detail is one explanation to investigate, not an established cause. If B also outperforms C, that would strengthen the interpretation that the generation stage adds little or removes useful information. A confidence interval spanning meaningful gains and losses is inconclusive, not evidence of equivalence. A sufficiently narrow near-zero interval would constrain plausible benefit for the tested setup, consistent with treating compression as a genuine trade-off [3, §7; 4, §4.5].
+
+**Business — brief Section 5 paragraph.** An adverse or sufficiently precise negligible result would support retaining structured features and avoiding an unsubstantiated generation, maintenance and monitoring expense. An uncertain result would support postponing expansion or collecting better evaluation evidence, rather than declaring the two approaches equivalent. This decision concerns predictive usefulness and operational burden; it establishes neither a financial loss avoided nor a causal business outcome.

+# Evaluation plan — Task 3
+
+**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh  
+**Course:** LLM4Rec, HSE University  
+**Dataset:** FAR-Trans  
+**Status:** Proposed, not executed. No recommendation scores, runtimes or costs have been measured for this experiment.

+**RQ1:** Do LLM-generated transaction-history summaries improve nDCG@10 for predicting future asset purchases compared with structured-history features for FAR-Trans users with sparse histories?
+
+The primary comparison is **Arm C minus Arm A** on the same pre-cutoff sparse-user cohort. Arm B and subgroup results diagnose that comparison. This plan follows official homework §§2, 4, 7–8 and 10. The class output is Top-10 and purchase-based nDCG@10; **the official split, candidate universe and eligibility rules remain pending**. All implementation defaults below are proposals, superseded transparently by those rules before final test evaluation.
+
+## 1. Temporal evaluation and future outcomes
+
+For prediction origin `t` and evaluation end `e`, propose:
+
+```text
+H(u,t) = permitted transaction records for user u with timestamp < t
+Y_raw(u,t,e) = distinct ISINs in Buy records with t <= timestamp < e
+S(u,t) = number of Buy records in H(u,t)
+```
+
+These are **event counts** for sparsity and **distinct-item sets** for relevance. Multiple future purchases of one asset give one binary relevant item, not extra gain. Sells may inform histories but are not positive purchase labels. An unpurchased asset is an unobserved purchase outcome, not evidence of dislike or unsuitability. Dates have no intraday order; the proposed whole-day boundary prevents the cutoff day's transactions leaking into that day's inputs. Do not use raw file order as a chronological split.
+
+Use one official train/validation/test schedule and one final test origin initially if the protocol permits. If multiple origins are required, use all required origins and report them individually. No date or six-month horizon is assigned from the papers. Before the official schedule is available, boundary/evaluator tests can use synthetic dates and fixtures; no provisional real-data split is to be advertised as the benchmark.
+
+### Training examples and label maturity
+
+Construct past user–origin examples `(F(u,s), Y(u,s,e_s))`, where every feature is built as of its own origin `s`. Fit using only examples whose complete outcome windows end before or at the validation origin. Select settings on an earlier validation window that ends before or at the final prediction origin. After selection, refit on the permitted train-plus-validation examples only if all their labels have matured by `t`. A training feature may never use transactions from its own future label window, even when both are earlier than final test time.
+
+Propose at most **three earlier non-overlapping supervised development windows** and **5,000 training user–origin examples**, using a seed-42 stable sample stratified by pre-origin Buy bands if more examples exist. These are compute-saving training defaults, not evaluation exclusions; use identical training IDs across arms. Use all official evaluated users and candidates, with no positive-injected test candidate sampling. If the official training schedule differs, revise and record it before looking at test scores. Keep final labels outside prompt-generation and feature-building code paths.
+

Separately apply official scoring eligibility, which may depend on whether there is a future label; do not confuse that condition with historical sparsity.
